That this House advise the children of Canada to write their letters to Santa Claus anyway and give them to their parents for transmission to their local member of parliament, who will give these letters to the Postmaster General for personal delivery to Santa Claus.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN FINANCING OF GAMES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the terms of Standing Order 43, I request unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with an important and urgent matter.
In view of the enormous deficit the Montreal Olympic Games are expected to incur, the fact that the Federal State of Germany assumed 48.6 per cent of the cost of the Munich Games, while the Federal State of Austria assumed 50 per cent of the Innsbruck Games, the fact that the Montreal Games may be in jeopardy, and bearing in mind that to date the federal government participation has entailed no real financial participation, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin):
That a quadripartite meeting be held by the federal government, the Quebec government, the City of Montreal and COJO with a view to finding an adequate solution to the problem.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN FINANCING OF GAMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to put a question to the Acting Prime Minister.
We are now in a position where we can more accurately assess the enormous cost of the Olympic Games and their deficit. Furthermore, we know the tremendous odds against which we are fighting to complete the program on time, make it a success and avoid waste.
Can the Acting Prime Minister tell the House whether or not the government is reconsidering its former position on this matter, in view of the fact that Canada's reputation is at stake and we do not want the Olympics to become for Montreal what New York City has turned out to be for the United States?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN FINANCING OF GAMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has been of substantial assistance

with regard to the Olympic games, first by providing certain federal services which are essential for security and for other aspects of the games. Through legislation we have also made it possible for very large sums of money to be raised by the sale of coins and stamps. If the hon. gentleman thinks we should go beyond that, we have not made a decision along those lines. Indeed, we stand by the position stated by the Prime Minister on many occasions that we will not be responsible for any part of the deficit of the games.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN FINANCING OF GAMES
speechtext:
I would like to ask a supplementary question.
Considering the Acting Prime Minister's answer, I wonder if he could tell the House whether or not the cabinet intends to deal with this most important question of a huge deficit and try to find positive solutions to help the province of Quebec concerning this situation which is most alarming for the people of that province, especially the city of Montreal?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN FINANCING OF GAMES
speechtext: As I said, we have acted in many positive fashions. If the hon. gentleman is asking whether we have made any decision to change the policy, the answer is no, but within the policy we have been of very substantial assistance to Montreal and to the success of the games.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Today I directed a question to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) in his capacity as minister in the House who answers for the anti-inflation board. I understand that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) answers for the legislation, but once the bill becomes operative and the board is in business the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs answers for the board. The minister ducked my question by suggesting it would be more properly directed to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan).
May I make the point that as the board becomes operative and more and more a matter of public concern, and hence a matter of concern to this House, we are entitled to ask questions about its day to day operations: these questions shall be directed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. My question today concerned the revelation made by the board yesterday that it had requested justification by CEMA of its most recent increase in the price of eggs. My question, with respect, was quite properly asking the minister what action he had taken in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, the misunderstanding is not due to the question asked. On the contrary, I am always happy to receive questions from the hon. member, but I noticed he rose to ask a supplementary and was looking for the Acting Minister of Agriculture in the absence of the minister.

Therefore, my reply to the hon. member had nothing to do with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) but rather with the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) who is Acting Minister of Agriculture.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order respecting an undertaking, as I understood it, made in the House by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro). About one month ago the Minister of Labour indicated, in response to an inquiry of mine, that the report of the commission with respect to the west coast grain handling problems in the port of Vancouver, the Bayda commission, would be tabled in the House, he said at that time, within one week or ten days. Subsequent to that we have had what is apparently a leak of the report, or parts of it, to the press, specifically the Vancouver Sun.

Subsequently I was assured by the parliamentary secretary that we would be having the Bayda report tabled. This is a matter of utmost importance and urgency as far as the people of western Canada are concerned and I would suggest, again, that if a minister makes an undertaking of the sort the Minister of Labour did, he should carry it out. We would now like to hear whether that report is going to be tabled now, or so far in the future that we can forget about any recommendations the report may contain?

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member that I did lead him to believe this report would be tabled sooner than has been the case. The only thing holding up the release of the report has been the deliberation of my cabinet colleagues in respect of certain provisions. It is our intention, as the government, to table the report together with our response to many of its recommendations in which I am sure the hon. member is interested. The consideration of certain elements of that response has been delayed due to the preoccupation of the government on other matters of higher priority: that is the reason for the delay. But I can assure the hon. member that as soon as the cabinet has had a chance to consider the material before it, we will make the report public. I do not anticipate that this will be too far into the future.

speechtext:
1.	Was Saint John chosen as the possible site for the proposed medium security prison in Martinon, New Brunswick and, if so, for what reason?
2.	Was the Northumberland-Miramichi area considered as the locale for such an institution and, if not, for what reason?
3.	Was the detrimental effect on a city like Saint John considered when the location for an institution of this type was being decided?
4.	Was a civic poll or study carried out to determine the attitude of the citizens of the area and, if not, for what reason?
5.	Have the plans been made public and, if not, for what reason?
6.	Has the Department of the Solicitor General given any consideration to the effect of escapes, riots, etc. on the population of the Saint John area which is possible due to the proximity of such an institution to an area with a population over 100,000?
7.	Was the unemployment rate in (a) Saint John (b) Northumberland-Miramichi taken into consideration in the decision to establish the prison at Martinon?

subsubtopic: SITE FOR PROPOSED MEDIUM SECURITY PRISON IN NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
1. Yes. To provide medium security facilities for inmates originating from the general area of Saint John, N.B., or wishing to re-establish themselves in this area upon release.
Order Paper Questions
2.	No. Since this area did not meet the Penitentiary Service criteria for the location of medium security institutions, in so far as this area was too isolated from a major urban centre.
3.	Yes. Based on experience with similar institutions in large urban centres, it was considered that it would have no serious detrimental effect on the City.
4.	No. However, the Penitentiary Service has applied to the City Council of Saint John, N.B., for authority to purchase land for the construction of such a penal institution. It was left to the City Council to determine the need for a public hearing since they are responsible for the management of the utilization of property within the boundaries of the municipality.
5.	No. The construction plans are not completed. However, the general concept plan was made available to the City Council.
6.	Yes. Such consideration is being given in the construction plans of these institutions. The construction plan will provide for appropriate perimeter security installations as well as the provision in appropriate competence and numbers of security staff to be employed not only on the perimeter security line but also inside the institution for the prevention of escapes and possible disturbances. In addition, it was considered that the few escapes that may occur in this type of institution would have an extremely limited impact on the community since inmates incarcerated in such institutions are not considered to be dangerous.
7.	Yes. The rate of unemployment in any area of this country is a constant matter of concern to all federal government departments. Accordingly, the government has taken measures to restrict unemployment to a minimum. However, in the location of penal institutions certain other factors of major importance must receive priority over unemployment if appropriate rehabilitation programs are to be conducted in an efficient and economic manner.

speechtext:
1.	Did the government recently sign an agreement with the Province of Quebec on immigration and, if so (a) on what date (b) for what purpose (c) what are its principal terms?
2.	Does the agreement permit representatives of the Government of Quebec, in Canada or abroad, to pass opinions or review applications of immigrants wishing to live in Quebec and, if so, what other provinces have similar privileges and signed agreements?
3.	Will representatives of the Government of Quebec be allowed to set up staff in Canadian diplomatic posts abroad for purposes of dealing with immigration and, if so, in what locations?
4.	Has the same privilege been offered to other provinces?
5.	Is the agreement intended to (a) promote French speaking immigrants to Quebec (b) discourage or prevent English speaking immigrants to Quebec?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: BIENVENUE-ANDRAS AGREEMENT
speechtext:
1. Yes. The Government signed a new Agreement with the Province of Quebec to replace the Lang/Cloutier Agreement signed in May, 1971. (a) The Agreement was officially signed October 17, 1975. (b) The Agreement outlines improved co-operative measures which the Federal and Provincial Government will use to encourage the movement of immigrants to Quebec, (c) The principal terms of the Agreement include the free exchange of information between Federal and Provincial Immigration
November 20, 1975

Officers that may assist in the recruitment of immigrants destined to Quebec, the opportunity for the Province to comment on potential immigrants destined to Quebec and the establishment of the staff of the Province abroad, their location and accommodation.
2.	Yes. The Agreement allows the Province to review applications of potential immigrants destined to Quebec or who in the opinion of the Canada Immigration Officer may be destined to Quebec and to comment on these cases. However, the final decision with respect to the selection of immigrants remains with the Federal Government. No other Province has signed a similar Federal-Provincial Agreement.
3.	The Province of Quebec may establish staff on a permanent or temporary basis in a Canadian diplomatic or consular mission where there is a Canadian Immigration capacity and where this is deemed possible or, if this is not possible, in a "Maison du Quebec" or elsewhere in cities where a Canadian Immigration capacity exists. Under the terms of the previous Agreement (Lang/Cloutier) the Province could request to have officers present in any Canadian diplomatic mission where this was deemed possible and during the life of the Lang/Cloutier Agreement the Province established officers in Athens, Beirut, Brussels and Rome.
4.	Yes.
5.	(a) The Agreement is intended to encourage immigration to Quebec of French-speaking or potentially Frenchspeaking immigrants who have the ability to integrate rapidly and successfully into Quebec and Canadian society. (b) No.

speakeroldname: Mr. Elmer M. MacKay (Central Nova) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
That this House, noting the public is concerned about recent disclosures of improprieties in the conduct of public affairs, as evidenced by events resulting in criminal prosecutions with respect to government dredging contracts, the Estey Air Canada inquiry, and disturbing reports about government leasing-concessions of airport duty-free shops, urges the government to take immediate action to restore public confidence in the government's efforts to control conflict of interest and other improprieties of public officials, most especially with regard to government contract and leasing procedures and practices.
He said: Mr. Speaker, during this opposition day motion I hope that apart from the normal amount of debate and controversy which this sort of exercise inevitably involves there will be an attempt to look objectively at certain procedures and habits involving leasing and consulting practices by the government that have developed over the years. I trust there are members of parliament from all parties who recognize that normal political patronage- which everyone who is a realist concedes is part of our political system-can, if allowed to remain unchecked and unsupervised, escalate into something that can become very ugly and to a great extent undermine the trust and credibility of any government under whose administration it is perceived to become rampant. Indeed, if allowed to become a way of life it can bring all those in public life into disrepute.
In discussing the matter of Sky Shops and Mirabel, which recently has been the subject of a good deal of editorial comment and news features in leading publications across the country and, indeed, mentioned extensively in parliament during the past few weeks, it is not my intention to overemphasize these particular situations but, rather, to use them as a focal point to discuss what I believe to be a wider and more important issue, namely, that some very sloppy practices and imprecise guidelines, together with a certain amount of favouritism, are prevalent today in the use of consultants and in the granting of leases and concessions by this government. I hope that speakers from the government side of the House will be able to tell us what progress is being made on the implementation of conflict of interest rules for senators


November 20, 1975

and members of parliament, and that we will not have the government House leader say, as he has in the past, that cabinet ministers should be subject to no more stringent rules in this regard than ordinary members of parliament.
I do not believe, however, that ministers, MPs or senators ought to be forced to divest themselves of all they have worked for while in private life simply because they have become part of our country's parliament. But there is a need for more comprehensive guidelines.
There seems to be, in my humble opinion, a lack of appreciation or perception by the government that the funds it administers must be used judiciously and that public property must not become the private preserve of the government's political friends. I think it is significant that I have had colleagues from different parties, including the one which governs our country, tell me they are not antagonistic to the course of action I have followed in focusing attention on matters such as the one I am going to discuss today which I believe to be politically improper and which involve an apparent lack of good judgment and business ethics.
Members of parliament who take an interest in the way that public properties are utilized and the terms of contracts involving governments can save the taxpayer a good deal of money. For example, I feel that a current exchange between myself and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) might serve as a good example of this sort of thing. This minister and I have been discussing a possible variation in the garbage contract for the city of Ottawa which involves the federal government. By reviewing the terms of bids which quoted different figures for the federal portion of the contract and by severing one of these bids from the contract, the end result may well be a saving of hundreds of thousands of dollars to the taxpayers of Canada. Should the Minister of Public Works feel he can take this practical course of action with the resulting saving, all of us, I am sure, with non-partisan views will commend him for it.
As far as Sky Shops, that suddenly famous duty-free establishment in Montreal, is concerned, a perusal of its financial records indicates that this firm paid substantially less than it should have, for several years, for the use of government facilities at the Montreal international airport at Dorval. Had a more realistic fate been assessed, comparable, for example, to that at the Toronto international airport for a similar establishment, Sky Shops could still have showed a very good return on its investment and the federal treasury would have been in receipt of a great deal of extra money from the lease of this public property.
I am convinced that at Mirabel, as well, proper bidding procedures were not followed and that a number of firms did not receive fair treatment when they submitted tenders for the privilege of operating a duty-free merchandising establishment there. In passing, one should look at the monopoly situation-a double-barrelled monopoly, in fact that Sky Shops enjoys: on the one hand, an exclusive right from the Liquor Control Board of the province of Quebec to sell, and on the other hand an exclusive lease from the Department of Transport, one monopoly dovetailing into the other and each justifying the renewal of the
Confidence in Government
other. This is not a very healthy situation. Perhaps the government ought to consider using its sovereign power to bypass provincial liquor boards and deal directly in cases such as this concerning the sale and distribution of spirits. That is something I think the government should consider.
Sky Shops is, as this House knows, a very interesting company. It appears that concessions were given by this organization in many forms. A senator, a former Union Nationale member of the Quebec legislature, made windfall profits quickly and for no apparent logical reason, at least based on strictly business considerations. It is obvious, as well, that Sky Shops was not reluctant at all to give certain prominent people favourable opportunities to acquire their stock at bargain basement rates. Customs officials, Department of Transport personnel and others received gifts from Sky Shops. To their credit, some of the recipients of larger gifts returned them, but that does not remove the need to scrutinize the motives of the executives of Sky Shops who, it would appear, are clearly in contravention of section 110 of the Criminal Code of Canada in giving television sets to federal employees, regardless of whether the sets were returned.
One has to question the motives of people who would put government employees in this sort of position. The fact, also, that P. Lawson Travel, part of the very considerable business empire of Thomcorps, paid what would appear to be an extraordinarily high price for the shares of Sky Shops which at the time was doing business at an airport soon to be over-shadowed by Mirabel, to which it would ostensibly lose its international flights, does nothing to dispel my feeling that part of the consideration was the knowledge that Sky Shops had the inside track on other duty-free operations which would be established in the future, particularly at Mirabel, and nothing in the ensuing course of events has changed my impression in this regard. I hope the government can do this. One of my colleagues will be developing this theme later.
Let us consider what happened to some of the other bidders who were unsuccessful in their attempts at Mirabel. I have one example of a man who in good faith endeavoured to obtain the duty-free concession at Mirabel in competition with some of the other nine bidders, including Sky Shops. I had a notary obtain a deposition, and the deponent, Mr. K. S. Kohli, is prepared to elaborate on it and to give other information if provided with a proper forum such as a judicial inquiry. However, I will quote some relevant parts of his statutory declaration and will be pleased to table the entire declaration, the original, if it is the desire of the House that I do so. One of the interesting things about the guidelines put out by the department for duty-free concessions is the fact that the department violated its own guidelines, something that does not exactly engender confidence in the system. The second paragraph in a Ministry of Transport publication reads:
The policy of the Department of Transport concerning the award of contracts for duty-free concession is as follows:
Once the bids have been evaluated, the department will advise each
bidder of the rank of each bid, in relation to the others.
This has not been done on several occasions. Perhaps some of the relevant parts of the deposition of Mr. Kirpal Singh Kohli, a Canadian citizen residing at 7910 Cote St. Luc, in the city of Montreal, province of Quebec, will

November 20, 1975
Confidence in Government
amplify some of the feelings of injustice that several people have conveyed to me as a result of the procedure. Mr. Kohli deposes and declares:
That I was a tenderer in response to the call of the Department of Transport of Canada for tenders for the duty-free shop concession at Montreal international airport at Mirabel in the province of Quebec.
I will not read all of this, Mr. Speaker, because it is fairly lengthy. He continues:
That upon the bids being opened and announced by an official of the Department of Transport, it appeared and I verily believed and do believe that my bid was the highest and the most remunerative to the Government of Canada and, indeed, I was congratulated as the successful bidder by certain of the other tenders;
That subsequently my tender deposit, being $20,000 in negotiable securities of Canada, was returned to me by the Department of Transport without explanation;
That knowing that the tender deposit should be retained until the tender was awarded, I inquired of an official of the Department of Transport for the reason why the deposit had been returned to me and I was informed that a mistake had been made and that the deposit should be returned to the Department of Transport;
That I returned the tender deposit to the Department of Transport in other negotiable securities of Canada in the amount of $20,000.
So he submitted that amount the second time. He goes on to say:
That on or about August 26, 1974, my tender deposit was again returned to me with a letter, as by reference to the copy of such letter, marked Exhibit A-
This is appended to the deposition. The letter simply states that the $20,000 was returned apparently for the second time and then goes on to say that the results of tendering for the duty-free shop will be announced in due course. Mr. Kohli finishes his deposition by saying:
That the letter mentioned in the preceding paragraph was the last communication I received from any official of the Department of Transport, contrary to the policy of the Department of Transport as set out in the document, of which a copy, marked Exhibit B, is attached to this my declaration.
That was the document in respect of the letter to which I referred a few moments ago. This paragraph is interesting, also:
That I was first informed that the Department of Transport has awarded the concession for the duty free shop at Montreal international airport at Mirabel aforesaid when comment thereon was made in the public press and other media following upon the presentation of a petition to the House of Commons of Canada on or about November 3, 1975-
These are one man's feelings. It may be said that he is exhibiting certain negative feelings because he was unsuccessful, but there is at least another bidder who had some interesting things to say. One of my colleagues will be dealing with this in due course. Some of the documents setting out the Sky Shops dealings over the years with the federal government are most interesting. We trust the government will table soon some of the more relevant letters and documents other than those which the opposition has supplied them. As the House knows, the situation outlining some of the rather unusual aspects of Sky Shops relationship with DOT and Senator Giguere has been a matter of public record since November 3. But at no time since then has the government tabled any documents which would shed further light on this matter. The government has gone into its usual defensive crouch.

I am sure Mr. Anton, the founder of Sky Shops, would like to testify before a judicial inquiry. This man, who founded the company and did all the work necessary to make it into a successful business, seems to have been a victim of his apparent requirement to surround himself with people who were politically acceptable. It is by no means certain that he did this voluntarily, and his reward ultimately was to lose control of his company and receive considerably less for his stock than the other shareholders. Frankly, I feel sorry for Mr. Anton who has a distinguished war record and appears to be hardworking and essentially a good type of person. But that is for another forum. Another thing troubles me about this particular aspect. It is exemplified in a statement made by, it is true, another unsuccessful bidder, but it is a statement that the man who furnished the information to me would be pleased to amplify were he given the proper forum in which to do so.
Many people involved have indicated their interest in testifying in what they perceive to be the proper forum. Clarence Campbell has made this remark, and Senator Giguere himself said something to that effect. In any event, such a remark made by a business associate to another bidder, a man who already operates a duty-free operation in Newfoundland, is very startling if it is true. While he was working on the bid, an associate of his, an acquaintance, came to him and said words to this effect.

This is worth investigating. We will never get to the bottom of this matter unless we have an investigation. Like Mr. Kohli, this bidder will, under proper circumstances, be pleased to provide more details. This type of remark, true or not, has serious implications.

speechtext: Did you say "true or not"? It has no implication if it is not true.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: That is why we want an inquiry.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Let us find out whether it is true or not. This type of attitude undermines the entire system.

Stick to facts.
November 20, 1975

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I am advised to try to stick to facts. I thank the minister for his advice, but at times we do not get much of an example from over there.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Tell us something else that is true or not.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I suggest that this type of attitude undermines faith in the system and that the attitude that the fix, or bribe, is the quickest road to success brought us the dredging scandal which, as all Canadians now know, is a multi-million dollar fraud.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Don't get excited.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Yes, don't get excited, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) says. Just relax. The philosophy of the fix, or bribe, must be stopped from spreading further, I suggest to the minister. How would we, as' members of parliament, feel if our elections were determined or were thought to be determined by any suggestion of bribery? Yet many people in the business community, rightly or wrongly, feel that their endeavours are governed by things like this; and the more this type of belief spreads, the more justification there will be to adopt this type of philosophy.
It is obvious that the government and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) do not know quite what to do, except to instruct the RCMP to investigate, and I commend them for this part of it. But there has been no tabling of documents, no statement by any minister on motions, not even a press release, and no indication that anybody intends to do anything but stonewall the entire matter and wait until the pressure subsides. There are suggestions that an RCMP investigation is sufficient. How ridiculous! No one can really believe that the types of questions that have been raised thus far in this affair, and will be raised by my colleagues and myself in the future, can be successfully considered, defined and discussed in the context of an RCMP investigation, however useful such an investigation may be to amass data and evidence. It is necessary to have a forum presided over by a distinguished jurist, assisted by able counsel for all interested parties, to consider a situation such as the Sky Shops affair.
We in the opposition consider it very strange that the government appears to take the attitude that we must apparently prove beyond a reasonable doubt that inquiries should be made. Where is the government's sense of responsibility? Have they no self-starting mechanism at all? It may be that after an inquiry and the ensuing report, the government can announce there was no wrongdoing at any time and that their methods of conducting business and dealing with matters such as those at issue today are so efficient and straightforward that they require no change in procedure. I, personally, hope that this will be the case. But I would like, for example, to see them explain certain contractual aspects of the Mirabel operation, even getting down to such fundamentals as to how people are put on planes. It is pretty basic, I would think, to the success of any airport. There are 13 or 14 passenger transport vehicles now at Mirabel each costing in excess of $400,000 and, as a matter of interest, manufactured by Booth Airside Systems
Confidence in Government
Incorporated of Pennsylvania, U.S.A., a subsidy of Booth Computer Corporation of California.
General Aviation, the company which has the contractual rights to operate these vehicles-the same company, incidentally, that had difficulty at Heathrow airport in the United Kingdom, reportedly because of labour problems- is not supplying technically competent people pursuant to the agreement they have with DOT, in that the operators of the PTVs are supposed to be the equivalent of experienced, heavy-duty equipment operators. I suggest to the minister that they are not. Late in October, for example, a PTV at Mirabel came in contact with a telephone pole and smashed a couple of cars. A small incident, but indicative. The operators and maintenance personnel are paid considerably less than their DOT counterparts and General Aviation makes a nice profit because of the comparatively low wages their men are paid.
Because of possible labour difficulties or other complications, one has to assume that DOT has provided back-up personnel to maintain and operate this equipment, since it is the only way to get people on the aircraft. It would be disastrous if that operation were disrupted. We know that the equipment is so unrelaible that approximately 14 machines are kept at Mirabel so that 8 or 10 of them have a reasonable chance of working at any given time. One has to ask why the Minister of Transport would countenance such a wasteful and stupid arrangement. Why do we need to have General Aviation operate these machines at all? Cannot DOT do the job? Also, why have these PTVs never been given a proper post-assembly check?
If the minister wants to know why at the official opening of Mirabel the PTV for the VIPs malfunctioned at such an embarrassing time, I can tell him. I leave to his imagination what is going to happen when these machines have to operate in the type of climatic conditions they will face during the winter. Is this the kind of expertise, in the conception of how to load passengers on planes, that approximately $50 million worth of consulting fees has achieved for Mirabel-

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
-an airport which, I suggest, is more like a gigantic reproach to reason than an airport. In this country we spend nearly $1 billion for consultants and outside services. Admittedly, some of these services, such as the Corps of Commissionaires, some teachers and accountants, are worthy and necessary, but it is the consultants themselves that disturb me. We pay approximately $5 billion a year for our public service, plus the money on consultants. Consultants have become a drain on this country. We cannot afford to have an expensive public service and an army of hangers-on, only some of whom are legitimate consultants, to help our public service do jobs they are being paid to do themselves.
It is interesting to look at the budget of some of our smaller provinces in relation to this type of budgeting by the federal government. Some of my figures may be a year old, some are based on projections, but they give a reasonable indication. I am not swearing to their absolute accuracy. In Manitoba, the current total provincial budget is around $1 billion; in New Brunswick it is less than $1 billion; in Saskatchewan it is a little over $1 billion; in

November 20, 1975
Confidence in Government
Nova Scotia it is about this amount; in P.E.I. it is $185 million; in Newfoundland it is almost exactly $1 billion. It horrifies me to see, in relation to what it costs to run an entire province, what this government is spending on consultants. It is interesting, also, to speculate whether, if the former minister of communications and chairman of the CRTC had been successful in Hochelaga, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would have hired a $40,000, $50,000 or $60,000 a year assistant to do the job that Mr. Juneau has been given. Would the job exist if Mr. Juneau had won in Hochelaga?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
If the Prime Minister had a business of his own and wanted to hire his friend and put him on the payroll, that would be a nice gesture indeed; but do the people of Canada need this political reject in the Prime Minister's office at this time of restraint? I think not.
I know the government is deeply embarrassed about Sky Shops, Senator Giguere, Mirabel and a number of other things, and I know that it has good cause for its embarrassment. My thinking has changed a bit during the past few days and I doubt whether there will be an inquiry. I say this for good reason. I think we may not have an inquiry because the government realizes that with all the facts which would come out, facts which the Senator probably knows, about patronage, the resulting scandal would be too much for even this government to bear. Under ordinary circumstances, and if the subject were not so delicate, there would be a good chance that an inquiry would be held, particularly in view of the number of newspapers and leading columnists who have stated unequivocally that this should be done.
Several months ago there was an inquiry into some aspects of Air Canada which I feel sure will ultimately prove valuable and constructive, and I once more compliment the former minister of transport for taking that course of action when he did. There were no RCMP raids, but there was an inquiry. Recently there was an inquiry announced into the Panarctic Aircraft crash, but the amount of agonizing that had to take place before it was done had to be seen to be believed.
In closing, I wish to say to the government that it should put its affairs in order, stop pending taxpayers' money on unnecessary luxuries as if our supply of money were unending and stop paying off friends with needless, nonproductive jobs. If the jobs are necessary and productive, no one will be disturbed if they are given to competent and honest Liberals-and there are many of them around; I am the first to admit that. No one ought to be upset in that case. But I say to the Prime Minister that, despite his recurring delusions of grandeur, I doubt if there is a serious economist in Canada who is not convinced that our present economic difficulties are caused to a large extent by the spending habits of the Prime Minister and his government.
If we are reasonably to expect Canadians to support the measures parliament is now considering to solve our economic problems, measures which require a considerable amount of self-denial by citizens of this country, this

government must show the way by its example. A good way to begin would be to make a diligent effort to find present abuses through an inquiry, curb them, and in future demonstrate more respect for proper business ethics and procedures in dealing with public properties and privileges.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I have carefully read the motion put forward by the official opposition and I want to say at the outset that it is a good motion. I particularly like some of the words in it; for example, "improprieties", which I will discuss later. I also wish to congratulate the hon. member who spoke for the official opposition. He is a good member of parliament; he does his homework.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: We all know that he is an honest man and that he will keep up the good work. However, I suggest to my good friend that although what he has been doing over the last number of months is good work, he should begin to realize that the things he has discovered which have occurred inside and outside government operations, both in the public and private sectors, are nothing more than symptoms of the kind of disease which is prevalent in our whole society. It is really a plague. It is not just peculiar to the party that happens to be the government, whether it be NDP, Liberal or Conservative.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: What was that first one?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
It is not just peculiar to one group of individuals in a particular sector of our society. It is a disease and a plague in our entire system. The hon. member has found improprieties. The dictionary defines "impropriety" as indecency, and it is very prevalent in our society. I am not one who is partisan, but whether a system is free enterprise, socialist, communist or whatever, in that system there must be an element of puritanism, an element of doing as well as we can at whatever work we do in an honest and equitable way, believing that there are rewards other than money and influence, such as appreciation and recognition for what we are doing. If a man stands shaving in front of the mirror in the morning and is able to look himself in the eye and not feel embarrassed but proud of what he is trying to do, whether it turns out that he is right or wrong, it is because he is doing as well as he is able to.
It may seem strange to some of my colleagues that I am trying to be somewhat philosophical about this. I am not trying to pretend for one moment that any one person, idea or system is perfect, or that no one ever made a mistake. The question is not what mistakes were made, but how they were made and for what motives. I wish to say quite bluntly and frankly that most of the world is governed and victimized by totalitarian systems and free enterprise systems, and those systems contain within them elements of greed, corruption, improprieties, or whatever other nice language one has to use in a motion before the House of Commons.
November 20, 1975

I will deal with our system because that is the one we live under. I would deal with the other systems if I were living under them, even at the risk of going to a labour camp. The mythology of free enterprise requires that profits be maximized and that we make all the bucks we can, as quickly as we can. It is all right to cut corners, to make mutually profitable deals and not to worry about who may be hurt. That is part of the system. Ethical businesses, ethical businessmen and ethical free enterprisers would be the first to turn down a case of whisky at Christmas time from business associates or competitors. They would not send a case of whisky to a friendly politician whether he be at the municipal, provincial or federal level.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: What about the socialists?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
If the system is so good-and I recognize the frailties and mistakes each and every one of us makes as individuals-it would seem to me the system would require that the mistakes are not made in that way. They would be genuine human mistakes of judgment, or even incompetence-which all of us are born with to some degree-but not mistakes of a case of whisky at Christmas, or sending a gift to a municipal councillor, an MLA or a member of parliament. I doubt very much if any member of this House has not had a gift offered to him at some time in his tenure as a member of parliament. Whether they have been accepted, I do not know and I would not presume to know. It is part of the system, part of the game.
I want to give full credit and honour to the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). He is an honest man, and is seen to be an honest man. Also, I am confident that the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and others on the government side are just as unhappy and concerned about this matter as anybody else. I am confident-and I hope my confidence is not misplaced-that they will carry out the most hardnosed inquiries possible and lay charges where they are required.
I am not going to cast personal aspersions against the Liberals or Tories, because I am not too happy about some members of the NDP either. We are all people. I condemn the kind of system that the hon. member for Central Nova represents, that members on the government side represent-going to church every Sunday and beating your neighbour the rest of the week. If you are to get ahead, the system requires that you be good at your job. That is not good enough for the so-called free society. If you have some friends and send a few cases of whisky, that gives you the jump on your so-called competitors in the free enterprise system. It is normal practice. But Air Canada may have been caught. If there were the accountability required of Canadian Pacific or other transportation companies who operate in Canadian airports as is required for Air Canada, I am sure the hon. member for Central Nova would have an even more interesting time than he is having.
I am glad this question has come to the surface and that the smell is getting around. Don't let us lay it at the door of Air Canada, however, or whoever may be in government departments, or contractors or dredgers or anybody else. That has been the name of the game since the turn of the
Confidence in Government
century. We just have to look around in our own communities, in our constituencies, amongst our own associates, relatives and friends, to see the state of mind and the attitude. If these free enterprisers think there is some value to the system that is worth saving, they had better hurry. The public is not going to stand for it. Each day more communists and totalitarians are created through the free enterpriser's conduct of his own affairs and the way he treats his fellow citizens. Think of the poor American bomber pilot who dropped another load on Viet Nam and commented, "I wonder how many more communists we created today?"
It is not what we say, but what we do, that counts; who we do it to, how we deal with people and with one another. Those right-wing reactionary dinosaurs who run loose in our society had better remember that if it is all right to hang the person who commits a premeditated murder or murders a police officer or jail guard who is on duty, it should be equally proper to hang the corporate president who defrauds people of $4,000 or $5,000 then gets a jail sentence of 18 months but only serves four months and goes home every weekend.
The poor slob who is unemployed and has a couple of kids, who knocks over a service station and steals a few bills, gets a three-year sentence and serves 18 months. Is it any wonder there is disrespect for the law, and cynicism? Is it any wonder people say, "To hell with you, Jack; I'm all right." That's what the system has taught them. Whether it is a civil servant in the middle or upper income levels, or a lawyer trying to get a contract for a company, or a corporation president, they are all caught at the same game. That is the fatal weakness of this so-called free enterprise system.
As a socialist, I will not take a back seat to the free enterpriser when it comes to the work ethic. The work has to be worth while, whether it be for Air Canada, or as a member of parliament or whatever-it has to be because you love the work you are doing. How much you get paid for it is secondary, as long as you get some recognition for it. About four or five years ago a businessman in Regina who was not a member of the NDP-he would not vote for me even if I were the only one running-sent me a letter, not a case of whisky or a pat on the back. He said, "I think you are doing your best at being a good member of parliament. You are working hard. I do not agree with much of what you say and do, but I thought I would write and let you know that I think you are doing a good job, even if I do not agree with the job you are doing." This man is a free enterpriser in the best sense of the word. It is difficult for me to concede good sense when it comes to free enterprisers, but this letter concerns the work ethic.
When I look at the word "improprieties" in the resolution presented by the official opposition, I think we all have glass roofs on our houses, as individuals, as parties and as a society. While it might be a great deal of fun to find some Liberals with their hands in the till, sooner or later some Conservatives and New Democrats and Credi-tistes will get caught. We are all part of the system. As an agnostic, let me say to all Christians: Let he who is without sin cast the first stone.
I hope the efforts of the hon. member for Central Nova will stir the government into taking expeditious action
9286

November 20, 1975
Confidence in Government
wherever there is impropriety. I hope those found guilty of impropriety will be treated under the law as the people expect.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hang them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I would agree with the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds). If a corporation president who has defrauded people out of $200,000 or $300,000 can get an 18-month sentence and then get out after three or four months and appear every Saturday night on "Hockey Night in Canada", it is no wonder people become cynical and say, "To hell with it". There is good reason. People whose politics are diametrically opposed to mine scream at me about law and order. They are the ones who are part of the system that allows such a corporation president to serve four months and then appear on "Hockey Night in Canada" every Saturday night, while the poor slob who has knocked over a service station gets three years. If the revelations of the hon. member for Central Nova result in people being found guilty of improprieties or breaking the law, I hope the fines and jail sentence will be in proportion to the enormity of the crime. The blue collar criminal is treated more severely than the white collar criminal.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: What is a blue collar crime?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I think the hon. member knows that as well as I do. There are blue collar criminals in his constituency. The fellow who knocks over a service station is treated more severely than the bank accountant who embezzles, the corporate president who defrauds and has lots of money to spend on his defence, and the senior civil servant who can disappear or travel to other parts of the world. The poor slob who knocks over a service station is given much harsher treatment than is meted out to our so-called leaders, to the white collar people, the mandarins, corporate presidents or members of parliament when they go wrong. As they ought to set an example, they should pay a greater penalty than the rank and file is called on to pay. That is all I suggest.
I don't suppose the men being investigated in connection with the hon. member's motion are any worse than others. Yet, for a change such crimes ought to be severely punished. I am not pleading for mitigation. I don't know why I should help free enterprisers who think our system is working so well. If they want to make their system as good as they say it is, they should forget about making all the fast bucks they can. They cannot forget Christian principles seven days a week, 24 hours a day. If they want to avoid totalitarianism in its worst form, of the left or the right, our free enterprisers had better change radically and deal with wrongdoers in their ranks as severely as they deal with other wrongdoers.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank hon. members for letting me talk a couple of minutes longer. If they are lucky, I shall talk no longer, as I must hurry to the airport to deliver passports to desperate constituents.
My philosophy considers what we can all contribute to society. It is not enough to be a puritan, a law and order man, to think as the dukes, lords and earls thought a couple of centuries ago. Such attitudes no longer work. If you are the head of a dredging company, a director of Sky Shops, a trade union leader, member of parliament, garbage collector, or the janitor of this building, when there is work to do, do your best no matter what your work is. The work itself is important, not how fast you can make the bucks or how quickly you can get ahead of the other guy. Greed is the motive of our system, and it will destroy us. The alternative will be a totalitarian system which none of us wants. It matters not whether you are a garbage collector; without your work, the city of Ottawa grinds to a halt. Everybody, from the Prime Minister down, needs the work of the garbage collector. It is important and noble work. Surely he should not need to give his union head or employer a case of whisky in order to get a better deal; yet that is what we do now.
We should all do our best work, not because we are paid but because we want to. We are not members of parliament for the pay. If we are criticized, often we deserve criticism. We are not here for the money, although we need money to keep balogna in the fridge and a few bucks to put away for our retirement. But that is not why we are here. The important thing is work for work's sake. I hope that does not make me sound like a puritan, because I am not. The point is, we must work because there is work to do, no matter what it is.
If the free enterprise system works so well, why cannot a reputable dredging company, or a company operating dutyfree shops, make an honest tender for an honest job? Why is it necessary to collude and bribe? Surely the reason is evident. I ask my friends on my right-I call them my friends because I like them as people-to think on this: for what do they stand? They support a system which will betray our nationhood and bring about the very difficulties which other countries have gone through. It will happen, if we are not careful, through conflict of interest, impropriety or whatever you call it. Consider what Karl Marx, Mao Tse-tung and Jesus Christ have said to use over these yea so many years. In the long run it matters not if we are Liberal, Conservative or NDP. What matters is our manner of living together, the society we create and how we treat one another.
The hon. member for Central Nova has worked diligently, as I said when I began my speech. But his findings
November 20, 1975

illustrate nothing more than how our social system works. He has merely discovered how a carpenter, president of a construction company or anyone else would behave in similar circumstances. No doubt the people involved in the business he investigated are basically good-as good as anyone else. But our system requires them to operate in the way they do. The situation is, if you want to get ahead, you had better make sure your company gets the contract. Do what you must to get the contract; that's the name of the game.
In case my friends on my right are overly enthusiastic later this evening, let me tell them that there is far less wrongdoing of this sort in public life, in governments, than in private business. But what is happening once in a while in government business is prevalent in private business, and has been for decades. We all know this to be the case, and no one should try to kid Joe Citizen about that kind, upright free enterpriser who goes to church every Sunday and tries to kick his neighbour in the backside the rest of the week.
There are some lessons to be learned here. Of course, improprieties in government and in public institutions must be continually scrutinized, and public accountability has always to be there. Let us require the same, not only of each other and of ourselves but also of the private sector. Maybe what goes on income tax returns, which are inviolate and confidential, may need a look at as well. The mood that we all know is amongst our citizens, our constituents, is there for a very good reason. There is cynicism, disrespect for the law, disrespect of leaders of whatever political stripe, and it is there for a very good reason. They have good reason for being cynical and disrespectful and saying to hell with the work ethic and to hell with enjoying the kind of work they do. It is because they have been educated since they were so high to make all the bucks they can, to get ahead of their neighbours. They have been brainwashed by deceptive and false advertising. Their priorities have been misplaced, like the government's. It is more important to worry about deodorants and snowmobiles than houses or pensions. They can increase the amount of money for the Secretariat of Intergovernment Conferences by $700,000 according to the supplementary estimates, but CMHC's land acquisition program received only $200,000.
Do you wonder why the citizen in Gopher Gulch, or Toronto, or anywhere else, is cynical and disrespectful when he sees $200 a day people sitting in Ottawa or Toronto, or reads about them in the newspaper and he cannot make a down payment on a house which he will never live long enough to pay for? Do you wonder why? What about our priorities, as well as our ethics? There is a reason people are disrespectful, resentful and cynical. All of us know this. When we go home to our ridings, we run into it all the time. It is frightening. Benito Mussolinis, Joe Stalins and Adolph Hitlers do not happen by accident.
So in the course of what we say in this debate, in the course of what the government will be doing-and I am confident they will be doing it expeditiously, honestly and fairly in terms of looking into improprieties-I hope we will all give consideration to our own priorities, our own work ethic and restoring some confidence and support amongst people generally, no matter what political or reli-
Confidence in Government
gious beliefs they may hold. If we do not do that, Mr. Speaker, what the hon. member for Central Nova has been working very diligently and well at will have gone for nought; it will have been pointless-because if you go back to 1870, whether it was Beauharnois, Sir John A. Macdonald, Wilfrid Laurier, or whoever we honour in our history, there is nothing new about this.
I would ask hon. members, again, whenever this happens in the course of wanting the free enterprise system to prevail, how many more totalitarians did you create in the course of carrying out the work of your system? If my hon. friends will do that, and if they succeed then, there will never be any need to elect an NDP government.

speechtext: Good!

I hope they will think about that. I thank my colleagues for their indulgence. What I have had to say may have been disjointed, but it is something about which I feel very strongly, and I know my colleagues do. I think all hon. members of the House feel that way.
All I am doing is asking, on behalf of my colleagues, that in the months ahead we take a look at what we are doing, at our priorities, at how we deal with one another, at how we deal with citizens, and at how citizens deal with one another under what is supposed to be a profit-motive system. If we took a good look at that situation, I suspect we could do much better.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member who moved the motion before us today for giving us the opportunity to discuss a subject which is extremely important to the good reputation of government and Parliament itself.
Indeed we were asked lately to discuss the restriction program advocated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to fight inflation. When I took part in this debate, I pointed out the distinction we should make between expenditures and waste. I would like today to emphasize for a few minutes the absolute necessity to prevent at all cost the waste caused by mismanagement, shameful patronage and the unnecessary spending arising from conflicts of interest.
Every year, the Auditor General exposes to the House the many inconsiderate and unwarranted expenditures which result in budgetary inflation. The recommendations of the Auditor General are practically never taken in consideration. Instead, the integrity and objectivity of this watchdog of government spending are sometimes questioned, even by the Prime Minister. It would seem that there is a certain premeditation as regards honest management of public funds. Of course, recent disclosures concerning contracts given to duty-free shops in airports are a typical example of what favours can be granted to political friends. Why do those things happen? Why does anybody not denounce them? Why are we deaf and blind when we know very well that this is happening? Why are there not duly mandated people working to prevent such situations? In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this suggests a certain tacit agreement among the authorities of the various departments, the civil servants and the shark friends of the party in power, that are always ready to bite into public funds. I
29956-36Vi

November 20, 1975
Confidence in Government
cannot see why it should be impossible to prevent such incidents.
It is therefore very obvious that this motion is timely. Action should certainly be taken immediately so that the public may have confidence in the efforts of the government to control conflicts of interest, wastage and unworthy patronage. This is particularly important and urgent since we only have to listen to opinions expressed by taxpayers to see how the honesty and integrity of the government, and so, of all members of parliament, are abused. Unfortunately, the bad opinion that citizens have about their representatives is caused mostly by this type of careless and partisan action on the part of the government administration. In these years where authority has been undermined, where respect and politeness are considered outdated, where disorder, if not anarchy, is increasingly present, it is important to see that it is necessary and even essential that the reputation of our leaders remain intact.
Only those who are respected can be obeyed. Only the authority of those whose integrity and honesty is above suspicion can be accepted. It is therefore our duty and obligation to restore the public confidence which the government sometimes help undermine dangerously.
Mr. Speaker, some might say that nothing in this is new and that unworthy patronage and conflicts of interest have always existed. I would reply that we must not wallow in the mud just because some of our predecessors have done so.
I am therefore in complete agreement with this motion, and I hope that the government will soon show its good will and good faith in trying to correct this sad situation. It is all very well to ask the citizens to tighten their belts, to make a personal, a voluntary effort to fight inflation, but they should not at the same time witness such wastefulness of public funds, all the more so that only a small fraction of the fraudulent transactions are made public. Therefore, to prove the determination of the government to put an end to those deplorable abuses, a widespread inquiry should be launched immediately, that the real culprits of those unacceptable manoeuvres be denounced.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring my remarks to a close by pointing out that the people would be driven to despair if the government were to continue to evade the issue. I sincerely believe in the honesty and sincerity of the vast majority of Canadians. It is often said that a people have the leaders they deserve. To my mind, I feel our people deserve better.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to start by saying that I am sorry the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) had to head off to deliver those passports to Regina before I could address a few remarks, through you, to him about his contribution to this debate. It is somewhat interesting that on a motion that dealt with proprieties of conduct in public affairs, he found it possible to address himself totally to the question of proprieties of conduct in private affairs.
I hope his colleague from Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) will convey a message to him. He thought it desirable to speak

some words in defence of the private enterprise system by way of giving it some advice. That was particularly touching since he is heading off to Saskatchewan, where not only does the provincial government, that belongs to the same party as he does, not think a great deal of the work ethic in terms of the ordinary sense of rewards and losses that go with it, but are setting a prime example of believing in taking from anyone who works and accomplishes something at any time that seems appropriate, leaving the losses with private individuals who put in their risk capital. I say that because it was a little strange to hear his flights of fancy about the private enterprise system, in face of that kind of endeavour.
The motion before the House was moved by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. McKay) and it raises a matter that members on all sides would want to take seriously at any time. The public is always concerned, and I am sure more so today than at almost any other period in our history, about the need for public affairs to be conducted in a scrupulously fair manner. They are insistent upon a high standard of conduct from government in the operation of matters of policy and the implementation of that policy. This government has been responding to that felt need by introducing a whole series of procedures and guidelines to assure, to the extent that it is possible to assure in any organization involving so many parts and so many people, that affairs are conducted according to the highest possible standards.
If there is increased responsibility on the part of government in this day to meet that proper public demand for high standards, I think there is also a high standard of responsibility demanded of politicians who represent constituencies in this House of Commons, particularly those who sit in opposition and who are therefore ordinarily engaged in criticizing and analysing. I think it is particularly important that in bringing forward criticisms or analyses, the most scrupulous conduct is in fact followed and observed.
I say this because there are some very important values in our society, and these values touch upon our very civil liberties: values such as the requirement of having proof before a proper court of law, the requirement of not subjecting persons to trial by innuendo or suggestion without charges first being established to the satisfaction of a law officer, whose duty it is to satisfy himself that there is the kind of case that warrants that kind of allegation to be put on the record. These are some very important principles, ones that I think all too often those who simply like to make news or to spread concern ignore at great peril to the foundations of our democratic and freedom-based system.
An inquiry of a broad-ranging nature is a technique that must sometimes be employed, perhaps to supplement other investigative techniques. But it is still true, and I hope members of the House understand this, that on the whole it is sound to allow investigative procedures to go forward in the usual way with experienced, trained investigators bringing forward matters for investigation, and then putting those matters in due course before a law officer of the Crown in order to decide whether specific action should be taken in relation to the matters originally alleged and now proved in a first-hand or prima facie way. These principles
November 20, 1975

were not lightly arrived at in our system, yet they are very important in protecting individuals who may be involved.
We have always, in this country of ours, been singularly fortunate in the quality of police investigation under the supervision of attorneys general across Canada and, indeed, in the quality of independence of attorneys general throughout the history of the country. That we have the best quality in these areas I think continues always to be important, and as we have them we should bear in mind that their strength of independence and integrity allows us to follow some of the time-honoured procedures that avoid the damage that can be done, damage both to individuals and, by the casting of innuendoes and aspersions abroad, to the system of government itself.
A government would be properly criticized at any time if it did not act promptly in relation to matters brought to its attention for investigation, whether it be misconduct, whether the police may be directly involved, or whether it be in the way of handling a particular matter or affair, in which case the proper road is to check the facts to see whether there was in fact an error, correct it where that can be done and take steps to assure that the system will avoid it happening again. These are the responsibilities of government.
We have before us a motion by the hon. member for Central Nova which refers to a number of supposed incidents requiring a degree of investigation and analysis.

I said to the hon. member for Central Nova, or about him, the other day that certainly compared to some of his colleagues-and I was at that point only putting it that high-he was one of the more responsible members of the House. I grant that in the ordinary course he in fact shows a high degree of responsibility. I hope that will continue to be the target for him, rather than to take advantage of a political opportunity to introduce confusion rather than light, attempting thereby to gain a political advantage rather than the real, important advantage of better public service through bringing direct attention to the problems which exist.
I was distressed when I saw a report the other day that he had said these matters had to be trotted out one at a time, one after another, rather than brought before the authorities, in a group in order that they could be properly handled and investigated. He wanted to bring them out one at a time in order that he could sustain the momentum of public comment on these activities. I say that is a wrong attitude and that any member who has information about any kind of misconduct, or any kind of information that is at all reliable, has a duty to bring that information immediately to the authorities for investigation, or to the government if that be the appropriate way of launching an investigation, or directly to the law enforcement authorities.
It must be an important duty of any member of this House and, indeed, any citizen of this country to bring that information forward at once. I think it was obvious that the hon. member for Central Nova brought forward some important information. In the case of Sky Shops, of course,
Confidence in Government
the government's direct involvement was in relation to the granting of certain leases, first at Dorval and then at Mirabel, which involved that company. The government was not itself involved in the question of shareholding or dealings in the shares of that company.
There may be questions that arise out of the evidence that has come forward in that regard and, as hon. members know, immediately that material was before anyone in authority an investigation into these matters was undertaken. Indeed, the investigation was under way before the information was brought before the House by the hon. member for Central Nova. That, surely, is the kind of responsibility this government has in relation to matters that look as though something may be wrong or there may be some problem of conduct in relation to any particular action.
The famous dredging contracts are referred to, again, in the motion; I might say "dredged up", again, in the motion, although what was involved there was not, of course, the allegation of any wrongdoing on the part of the government. I would appreciate it if hon. members opposite would assist in the process of analysing the problem by saying that there was no evidence of any wrongdoing whatsoever on the part of the government in relation to dredging, but that certain matters are now before the courts as a result of investigations which were launched, again by the government. These investigations were begun before the allegations were put before the House by an hon. member opposite.
In terms of public duty, what the government has done in a case like that is to see that an investigation takes place, to see that if there are charges to be laid they are then laid by the appropriate authority, which very often is the attorney general of a province when criminal law is involved, rather than a federal minister who does not ordinarily enforce criminal law. That is an example, I think, of the execution of proper diligence on the part of the government in relation to a matter which arose as a problem.
As I say, it would be appropriate and I think it would be desirable, in the interests of understanding, when public authority is under attack and when there is a real sign of a problem or lack of diligence, that in those cases where there is no evidence of such an act it is noted by hon. members. Then there would be the avoidance of what in this motion seems to be an interest in a particular situation which the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre could properly point out to the private sector and which does relate to the public sector.
Again, I suppose the reference to Air Canada and to the Estey report is of a somewhat doubtful nature in a motion relating to the conduct on the part of the federal authority although, of course, the corporation in question is a Crown corporation. Again, I know of no allegation on the part of anyone of any wrongdoing by the government. There were allegations or questions raised about certain matters or certain transactions, and the moment these came to light and to the attention of the government something was done. Indeed, in that particular case an inquiry specifically into the transactions-because it was, indeed, a Crown corporation-was instituted and a report in relation to that matter will be available as soon as it can be made public.
