I have said, Mr. Speaker, that generally speaking the hon. member for Central Nova shows a high degree of responsibility. I note some instances where that sense of responsibility seems to have failed him in the pursuit of these particular matters. I wonder, for instance, what led him to introduce the other day in the House of Commons- on November 13, I believe-in a question relating to the production of papers, the reference to a supposed sugar transaction in the Barbados by an official associated at that time with Air Canada. The matter itself had in fact been investigated to the extent thought desirable by the Estey commission. There is no suggestion, in the reference, of any responsibility even by the management of Air Canada, let alone by the government, yet it was introduced in this spurious way.
I saw another reference to political donations having been made by a company involved in bidding on contracts. It turned out, of course, that the donation referred to was by an unsuccessful bidder, yet it was all wrapped up in terms of some kind of innuendo and allegation without anything being carried through. I think that is unfortunate. This is, of course, the very kind of question that can be raised and that this government has helped to put behind all of us involved in the political process with the introduction of new election expenses legislation and a totally new approach thereto so there can be no grounds for that kind of suspicion.
There is, again, an allegation in relation to gifts to certain employees of the government. Again the law is clear, and the appropriate approach in cases of any such indication or allegation is an investigation. Certain similar instances came to the attention of the government some years ago in relation to certain employees of the government. An immediate investigation was launched and as the investigation proceeded, the evidence, as is our practice, was turned over to the appropriate provincial attorney general for appropriate action.
The law is clear in the Criminal Code that gifts are not to be accepted by civil servants, from anyone, without the express, written consent of the head of the department. That is clear, it is strict, and it is a rule that has needed to be re-emphasized throughout the civil service. As a result of that particular series of incidents in 1972-73 a new set of directives was issued reminding civil servants of the strictness of that ruling, and reminding deputy heads of departments of the need to comment upon it in any way they felt necessary or desirable for the guidance of civil servants. This is another case where, therefore, the whole of the case is made to mesh with other things without quite being clear.
I do not know why the hon. member for Central Nova, in this motion, went into the question of whether or not the PTV vehicles were working superbly at Mirabel airport. This strikes me as another red herring. The information I have is that they are being competently operated. He referred, with amusement, to the one which did not operate at the time of the opening of Mirabel and suggested some mechanical incompetence. I am told that in fact a fuse blew on that occasion. It may be worthy of a small investigation, but hardly the linking of that with other matters as the hon. member has done.
Perhaps worst of all today was the linking by the hon. member of allegations and discussions he has been putting before the House with respect to not only a hearsay statement but a hearsay statement reporting a hearsay statement which he attributed, after I requested the name, to the first individual who reported the hearsay to him. That is the kind of statement which surely deserves, if anything, police investigation. If it has the kind of relevance that deserves an investigation, it is the kind of thing that should be followed up in that way. Anything that can be stated by that person, or a source that can be found through that person, can be followed up by the police without these matters being put in an innuendo way, without any proof or follow-up, before the House and by persons who may, as in the case of several of the persons to whom the hon. member referred, have some reason for bitterness about not having been successful in a tender process.
The hon. member referred to the particular case of a Mr. Kohli. If it is true-and I will check that fact also, since so many of these thing turn out not to be true upon examination-that Mr. Kohli never had explained to him why he did not receive consideration of his tender, then it may be that there was some impoliteness and our procedures, in order to be perfectly polite, should be improved.
But it is clear that Mr. Kohli's tender did not in fact qualify within the grounds of tendering. The square footage to which he was referring in his tender was totally different from the square footage that was available and involved in the request for tender. It was for that reason his bid was not considered among, I think, the seven or eight which were left for consideration.
The way in which a particular bidding situation goes on is perhaps always complex. When the hon. member for Central Nova referred to the extension of the Dorval contract for the first time in this House, when the contract was extended to Sky Shops for an additional five-year period several years before its time ran out, it appeared to everyone to be a peculiar circumstance. Upon investigation it was discovered that the reason was the need for some construction to make the operation a reasonable one. Construction would take a certain period to be depreciated. The operation was one that existed in the Dorval airport in respect of a duty-free shop, a shop which would be less than significant once international traffic was transferred away from Dorval, and the plan was to transfer it from about 1974-75 to Mirabel from Dorval.
With that explanation, the mystery vanished and the situation was in fact a clear one from the point of view of the conduct of the department and the people involved in this transaction. It turned out that in that particular contract the renegotiation involved the raising of the rent which had to be paid by the lessee, even for the remaining three years or so, on a lease where from its inception he had a much lower rate of percentage to pay in relation to his gross revenue.
The case of the Mirabel contract has been raised. Here again, as I have said to hon. members, I will be very glad to discuss the question in detail, particularly in the forum which I believe is most appropriate, a committee of this House where cross-examination can take place and where witnesses can be present and examined. I do not under-
|Mr. Lang.]
November 20, 1975

stand hon. members not wanting that kind of forum, when obviously they want to cross-examine. They appear only too eager to make some comments, although it is a little difficult to hear even what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) is muttering at this particular point in time with regard to this issue.
Before a committee of the House I will be very glad indeed to look at the particular contract and the granting of the concession at Mirabel. As was said before in the House, it was a situation where an analysis of the tenders showed there were different levels of tenders and different levels of the likely rate of return on the basis of the percentages which were offered by way of rent for the service. A couple of issues which are pretty important were involved in that particular granting of tender. One of them was referred to by the hon. member for Central Nova when he said that it has been the practice, in the granting of duty-free shop concessions in relation to liquor, to pay attention to the licensing authority in the province in which the international airport is in fact located.
I think that particular consideration does deserve reexamination. I have asked that we re-examine the question of whether or not the tendering procedure should be related in any way to the licensing provisions of the provincial liquor licensing authority. Hon. members will appreciate how it may have come about that the provincial authority generally in charge of licensing for the sale of liquor was given the consideration of being the licensing authority as well at international airports. I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Central Nova, that constitutionally that is not required; but having in mind federal-provincial relations, it was an understandable development.
It is in that way, for instance, that at the Toronto airport the duty-free shop for liquor is actually operated by the Ontario Liquor Board and there, as I understand it, this was done without tender and through negotiation because of the specific desire on the part of that liquor board not to have anyone but itself involved in that sale. I think that matter does deserve review because it had an impact upon the tendering process in the Mirabel case. It led, indeed, to a conclusion that one particular bidder, largely a foreign-owned bidder, should not be considered as one of the contenders for the contract because of the policy of that particular provincial liquor board which required a higher degree of Canadian ownership than that for a successful bid.
I am not trying to forecast how we, as a federal government, would or should have concluded that particular matter, or what conclusion we should have arrived at concerning whether or not a foreign bidder should have been acceptable. But I do say that in that particular case it was a consequence of relying upon the approach of the provincial liquor licensing authority that led us not to seriously consider that particular bid along with the others which were evaluated and re-evaluated with a good deal of care by a committee of officials before one bid was selected.
Mr. Speaker, in short, I say to hon. members that we have attempted at every point we can to pursue investigations into any matters which are brought to our attention about problems, whether they indeed be picayune, or a particular vehicle not operating up to complete standards.
Adjournment Motion
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that earlier hon. members were having some fun over whether or not the runways were properly built. Investigation confirmed to me that they are in fact of a very good standard indeed. That kind of red herring is pursued by us as we try to cater to the particular whims of members opposite regarding what should be investigated.
When it comes to more serious matters, matters of alleged impropriety, then I think that not only must we act with dispatch but it is important that hon. members opposite, as any citizen in this country, co-operate by bringing to the attention of the authorities all the information they may have that bears on the question, and bring it forward as quickly as possible. Then, when investigations are appropriate, this government will ensure that they are carried out with dispatch. In the ordinary course we will rely on the procedures of investigation by law enforcement officers, and if criminal matters are involved we rely upon the decision of officers of the Crown, attorneys general in this country, as to the steps that should be taken with regard to that matter.
We will not want, ordinarily, to share with hon. members or in any way to approve what hon. members may do if, by using this House as a forum and a protection or in any other way, persons are smeared by innuendo or involved in a trial of reputation without a proper investigation. That is not according to the traditions of this country and of our system of law, and I urge all hon. members to co-operate with us in ensuring that the proper steps will be taken and that proper investigations will be carried out. On behalf of this government, I can assure hon. members that whenever matters are brought to our attention the appropriate investigation and action will be taken, and we will always be glad to lay that action record before hon. members and before the public and to stand on it.

November 20, 1975
Confidence in Government

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. MacKay:
That this House, noting the public is concerned about recent disclosures of improprieties in the conduct of public affairs, as evidenced by events resulting in criminal prosecutions with respect to government dredging contracts, the Estey Air Canada inquiry, and disturbing reports about government leasing concessions of airport duty-free shops, urges the government to take immediate action to restore public confidence in the government's efforts to control conflict of interest and other improprieties of public officials, most especially with regard to government contracts and leasing procedures and practices.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I heard the sanctimonious utterances of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) a few moments ago and I am sure there was not a dry eye in the House. It reminded me very much of the statements that were made in another capital city not too long ago by the president of that country who spoke with equal sanctimoniousness about those things which he said did not exist.
The minister has had to leave the House to go to an appointment, and I understand that; but I want to ask him, through you, Mr. Speaker, about a couple of the statements he made. He indicated that the government moved with great speed in the case involving Air Canada. They appointed a very reputable high court judge in Ontario to investigate that case. I want to ask him what is the difference between that case and this case, in terms of the obligations that are before the public. What caused the government to move so quickly in that case, and what has caused them not to move so quickly in the Sky Shops matter? What is the difference? I suggest there may well be a significant difference, the difference being that somewhere in the net is caught one of their own.
When the Minister of Transport talks about the equal hand which he will apply to each case, I say to him that he is talking as if he were Otto in Wonderland, because that is not the case at all. There is perhaps a difference between the Air Canada case investigated by Judge Estey, a good investigator appointed with such speed, and the case involving Mirabel with which the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) has been dealing. In the Mirabel case, the police saw fit to raid the office of a senator in this building and they saw fit to raid his home. That is a considerable difference and it adds another element in this case.
I am saying to you, Mr. Speaker-and let there be no doubt about it-that if there was justification in the case investigated by Air Canada through Mr. Justice Estey, then this case involving a member of the Senate cries out for investigation and for action. There are differences, and let us not fool ourselves in this place that a defence can be made to a legitimate request by a member who is generally regarded as having performed a heroic act in bringing forward this case with such restraint. Let us not be fooled that any defence can be made by attacking the integrity of the hon. member for Central Nova.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner (London East)).]
The minister spoke of civil liberties a few moments ago, and of the right to protect them. I agree with him; there is not a member of the House who would disagree with him. But one of the liberties of a free citizen in a free society, in a parliamentary system, is the right to the truth. I am saying to you, sir, and to anyone who would defend the stonewalling that has gone on in the House in the question period, and lately by the Minister of Transport, that it is denying not only to the House but to the people of Canada the right to the truth. It is about time we stopped doing that and realized that the House is not a place where before a member can stand up he must prove his case beyond a reasonable doubt. The Parliament of Canada is not a court of law and it is not a public inquiry, but when a member of parliament brings forward information such as the information that the hon. member for Central Nova has brought forth, then the government has a duty to act, not to evade or avoid because one of their own may be caught in the net. They have a duty to give more than the lip service just given by the Minister of Transport on the guidelines of conflict of interest. The papers on the guidelines on conflict of interest have been stuck in a committee for over a year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: That is not so.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
If I am wrong, please correct me. That delay almost provides the grease for the skids to make respectable the avoidance of responsibility which the hon. member for Central Nova has asked this government to take, and which they have refused to take thus far. From what the Minister of Transport said today, they will probably continue to refuse. Let there be no doubt about it, they do a disservice to themselves, to this parliament, and to the whole idea of public trust in public life. Let us make no bones about it, and let us call it what it is. It is important, because it is the very foundation stone of parliamentary government, that it be operated by reasonable men of integrity, that everyone act reasonably, and when situations cry out for investigation that they be investigated. It is an important relationship.
On December 10, 1974, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) put this relationship forth very succinctly. He said the following:
We do not live and work in times when the public feels really confident about any so-called honour system which is supposed to be operating in politics and in high levels of government. Why encourage further erosion of that confidence, when the appearance of proper guidelines could start to turn things around and help to restore some confidence? Public confidence is a precious commodity, almost as precious as democracy itself, because without it the democratic system just cannot work. To encourage it requires firm action and proper priorities.
The confidence of the public has not been encouraged, and firm action and proper priorities have not been forthcoming with respect to some of the matters in this motion. The Giguere question, the findings of the Estey report, and the SIU situation all point to examples of the way the Liberal government has allowed public confidence to be undermined.
This parliament has dealt with conflict of interest guidelines to a limited extent. The conflict of interest guidelines have been set forth as follows:
November 20, 1975

Conflict of interest denotes a situation in which a member of parliament has a personal or a private pecuniary interest sufficient to influence, or appear to influence, the exercise of his public duties and responsibilities.
The proof of conflict of interest in this particular instance rests on the monetary or material gains influencing public or political decision making. The case of Senator Giguere brings into question not only the impropriety of a member of the Canadian parliament, but also the inability or ability of representatives to distinguish, at least in some instances, between the public and private interest.
Again the government has offered no leadership. For a Canadian Senator to accept stock transfers at almost an honorific price from a company whose contract is exclusively contingent upon government decisions not only raises the question of conflict of interest, but also casts in doubt the ability of a member to discern what is a conflict of interest. There cannot be any denial of that, even though many of us would like to say that we could deny it. In short, even if the minister is not culpable, and even if he did not know there were huge monetary gains to be made from such a stock transfer, the situation should never have been allowed to happen. In that it did happen, and in that the government's own guidelines do not make it clear what is a conflict of interest, the government itself becomes culpable of undermining the public trust, of which I spoke, and to which the minister gave lip service just a few moments ago.
It has been admitted by the government that the provisions which have operated heretofore are both outdated and woefully lacking in meeting with public expectations of governmental integrity. At present members of parliament are prohibited from accepting fees relating to any matter before the House, from entering into contracts with the government, from holding shares in a company which wins a public works contract, and from voting on a matter in which they have direct pecuniary interest. There is no mention of stock which the family of a member of parliament may hold. At present there are no official regulations requiring disclosure of interests.
Perhaps this government has not been the best, but another prime minister dealt with the situation. In 1964 the late Prime Minister Pearson attempted to set down a code of ethics for his ministers and their departments to follow.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: After a whole bunch of scandals.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
After significant
trouble, as a matter of fact. I will quote from a letter he wrote to his cabinet colleagues as follows:
It is by no means sufficient for a person in the office of a minister-or in any other position of responsibility in the public service-to act within the law. That goes without saying. Much more is required. There is an obligation not simply to observe the law but to act in a manner so scrupulous that it will bear the closest public scrutiny. The conduct of public business must be beyond question in terms of moral standards, objectivity and equality of treatment.
How does that stand in the face of what we know and in the face of what has been disclosed by the hon. member for Central Nova? How do we justify the fact that this paper on conflict of interest guidelines is still stuck in the morass of our committee system? In the case of Senator Giguere it is well known that he is intricately involved in Kebec Restaurants and AFC Limited. These two organizations
Confidence in Government
are inextricably bound up in the transportation industry and with government tenders.
When asked if Senator Giguere was violating the present guidelines on conflict of interest, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on November 5 replied, and I quote:
-it is not apparent to me that there has been conflict of interest.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: How would he know?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I ask the question, how would he know? This stance, and the statement of the Prime Minister are indicative of the weakness and inadequacy of current government proposals and of the nonchalant fashion of the government in handling this issue.
With regard to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), he said he was looking after the interests of his constituents. He claims that when he was acting as principal secretary to the Prime Minister he handled the Sky Shops request in a manner similar to that in which he would have handled any constituent's request.
If the government House leader or the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) will not remind him, the minister should be reminded of the position of Lester Pearson and the Liberal government on this matter. I quote again from the letter of the former prime minister:
In order that honesty and impartiality may be beyond doubt, members of Ministers' staffs, equally with ministers, must not place themselves in a position where they are under obligation to any person who might profit from special consideration or favour on their part, or seek in any way to gain special treatment from them.
In turn, if the Prime Minister claims that he gave his secretary the go-ahead-and apparently that is what he did claim-I should like to remind the House of what the late Prime Minister Pearson said about that kind of activity. He said the following:
It is perfectly proper-indeed it is desirable-for members of ministers' staffs to be responsive to complaints as to delays in procedures or unfairness of treatment. They should bring these to the attention of the minister, or to that of the proper officials in a department. But in no case must a member of a minister's staff-or any other public servant- seek to gain for a particular person treatment that would not be accorded to any citizen .. . There can be no special treatment on the ground of personal acquaintance, sympathy or anything of that kind. Least of all must there be any suspicion of special treatment when there is cause to believe that a violation or evasion of law may be in issue.
What I am saying is that there is sufficient evidence in this case to ask to what extent there was involvement, and to demand an answer with respect to this matter, having regard to the involvement of the particular member of the other place with the matter in question.
We have demanded action on conflict of interest matters. This is the second time this party has allotted an opposition day to this subject. Other parties have also shown concern. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has a bill on the books respecting the disclosure of financial interests by senators, members of the House of Commons, and certain other persons. I hope it does not die a slow death, or I hope its death is much quicker than the breathing into life a public inquiry on this matter has proven to be.
Confidence in Government

November 20, 1975
I challenge the government to undertake its obligations for the sake of this institution, the members in it, and every public person whose name has become involved-for the sake of the other place and its integrity. I say do not attack the hon. member for Central Nova as your defence. Do not rely on the sophistry of that kind of defence. I ask you to take your courage in your hands and, for the sake of those other things I have mentioned, bring on a public inquiry before a judge. We would be satisfied with Chief Justice Estey or any other reasonable judge. Do not tell us that disclosure to a parliamentary committee under our rules means anything but a continuation of the kind of stonewalling that has gone on here in another form.
Is there any member of parliament who will say he is opposed to a public inquiry? Is there any member of parliament who knows something about the case that we do not know that would make him opposed to a public inquiry? If anything is wrong, open the books; if anything is wrong, investigate; if anything is wrong, find out. Do not sit on your hands and attack a member of parliament for bringing forward something which it was his duty to bring forward. That, however, is the whole of the case of the government, Your Honour.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was my intention in participating in this discussion to try to limit my comments to the function I serve as chairman of the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections and, pursuant to the motion of the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), to take up some parts of the subject of conflict of interest. The hon. member has since left the chamber.
Before I go into any detail in this regard I should like to bring to the attention of the last speaker, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), that he may have some concept of the conflict of interest legislation in the Canadian House of Commons that is significantly different from my own, and possibly different from that of a number of other individuals.
First of all, to correct the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, the conflict of interest legislation has not been stuck in any committee for a year. It was referred to committee on December 10, 1974; there were 21 meetings at which, as the hon. member should know, a considerable amount of effort was put in by all members, and the committee's report was tabled in the House on June 10, 1975.
The second correction I should like to make to the hon. member's remarks is that the conflict of interest guidelines are not government guidelines any longer; they are recommendations of an all-party committee which unanimously supported them together with the amendments and the deletions which we proposed.
The third correction is that unfortunately the hon. member is of the opinion there is no legislation which proscribes the holding of stock in certain companies by individuals related to members of parliament, whether of the House of Commons or the Senate. I can assure him that there is indeed such legislation, and the conflict of interest guidelines proposal No. 11 specifies these matters at great length.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: You make my case stronger.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I agree with the interjection of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton. He has been trying to make his case stronger. If he deems it suitable to refer to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) as "Otto in Wonderland" he will not object to being referred to as "Wallie in Wonderland".
I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, that I wanted to restrict my comments to the area of conflict of interest because of the work of the committee, and hopefully to make such comments a contribution to the discussion whether for the benefit of interested members generally or for the public.
My initial comment would be that, give or take the varying comments made on either side of the House, including those of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton to the effect that this side is attacking the hon. member for Central Nova, I should like to suggest the opposite.
I happen to represent the riding in which is found the city of Dorval. If the hon. member for Central Nova were here he would confirm that we have had some discussion on a shared interest in this problem. Hopefully these discussions will result in a solution.
The motion reads in part:
-urges the government to take immediate action to restore public confidence in the government's efforts to control conflict of interest and other improprieties of public officials, most especially with regard to government contract and leasing procedures and practices.
I would just say that members who are interested in pursuing the subject will find that the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections did go into that topic in considerable detail. The recommendations go substantially beyond those laid out in the original green paper on conflict of interest.
I should like to assure all hon. members and the public that some of the most stringent regulations to be found in any western democracy are in the Canadian conflict of interest legislation. It is my understanding that the legislation in the form of amendments to existing laws, as well as new legislation, will be ready some time next spring.
That brings me to a problem which has been referred to by the Minister of Transport and in relation to which any discussion of conflict of interest deserves at least a momentary review.
One of the remarkable problems we face in the House of Commons and in the news media is the apparent capacity, whether it be by members or the news media, to level accusations without fear of having the same burden of proof or responsibility placed upon the accuser as is placed upon the individual who is accused.
I make no suggestion that such is the case in the remarks made earlier today by the hon. member for Central Nova. I do point out, however, that we face a significant problem if we permit the general principles of justice, which have guided our courts over centuries, to be abandoned in favour of changing the forum or arena either to members acting by themselves or as members of the House of Commons, or to trial by the news media. In both cases the accused has no opportunity for a reasonable, fair hearing. I do not know of any way we can limit this right on the part
November 20, 1975

of members, but I do not think anyone would want to limit them in raising matters such as the Dorval and Sky Shops affairs.
I would remind the House that a free press and free news media have meant publications like the National Inquirer, and others which most of us would agree are less than tasteful, and which do not accept some of the responsibilities that go with a free press. We support a free press on the grounds that it is the best way to get the best possible contribution from an independent press.
In the same way, I think we have to support the concept of the investigations carried out by the hon. member for Central Nova, but always with the understanding that it is a privilege given to us to accuse without danger of retribution. If we abuse such a privilege, then we will be guilty of something called muck raking.
Other than that, I want to assure hon. members that other areas were covered in the matter of conflict of interest. According, in my view the government's action to date meets the demand of the motion which asks the government to take certain action.
We have spent considerable time studying conflicts of interest. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) said so well in the question period one day, political practices acceptable ten or 20 years ago are no longer acceptable. The difficulty with drawing guidelines to cover conflicts of interest is that our views on conflict of interest are constantly changing. It is difficult for members of the House at large, those serving on the committee on Privileges and Elections, the media, or the public to agree at any one time on what constitutes improper behaviour, or what proper behaviour ought to constitute.
I note that the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) suggested to the Procedure and Organization Committee this morning the establishment of some procedure in this House to provide for quick impeachment of members. Possibly that is one technique the House ought to consider.
Amendments to be brought forward, either in the form of amending bills or new laws, will prohibit the holding of dual electoral offices, prohibit the members' or senators' participation in any contract made with any government in Canada, prohibit the participation by members of parliament and senators in the management of any company which has entered into a contract with a government, require members of parliament to declare their interest in any subject matter under debate, and prohibit members from voting on a bill with respect to which they have an interest. I underline and stress strongly, for the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton who has alluded to this subject, that, without question, the regulations will pertain to the families of members of parliament and of senators.
In order to assure the population that members of this House are determined to be guided by such regulations and laws, we have suggested guidelines which will recommend that any citizen of Canada may go to the Federal Court and ask the court to examine any particular issue which relates to the behaviour, or participation in any contract, of a member of parliament or senator. The law will require the attorney general of the province to proceed with the
Confidence in Government
case, on its merits, on behalf of the citizen; should the attorney general refuse, the court will be obligated under the new law, to report the action to the Speaker of the House of Commons or to the Speaker of the Senate.
As I was surprised about comments made on the government's stand on conflict of interest, I shall read to hon. members a number of suggested provisions contained in the report tabled by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. The part I shall read is headed "Financial Interests". It says, as recorded on page 24:5 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections:
It is recommended that the proposals entitled: 'Financial Interests' be expanded to the 'Office of Registrar', whose existence is intended to assure the public of the determination of members of parliament to avoid potential or actual conflicts of interest.
Here let me correct a misapprehension raised by the hon. member for Central Nova concerning regulations and restrictions which ought to apply to members of the House and senators. The hon. member suggested that the guidelines applying to ministers will not be more strict than those applying to members. His information is not correct. The guidelines for ministers will be more strict than those with respect to members. I continue quoting:
Your committee agrees with the statement in the green paper that 'Members may increasingly find themselves in situations for which no adequate rules or guidelines exist to aid them in ensuring that their conduct respects their fiduciary duty'.
Accordingly, your committee envisages the function of the registrar as being:
(a)	The registration of an annual statement of the pecuniary interests of each member of parliament, and the making and filing of records pertaining thereto;
(b)	The provision of confidential advice to members of parliament, at their request, on any matter that may concern a possible conflict of interest of the member.
(c)	The annual reporting to the House of Commons of a list of those members of parliament who have complied with the requirements of the law relating to registration and/or disclosure.
To assure the public that members of parliament will indeed take the steps necessary to avoid conflicts of interest, your committee recommends that the draft legislation and where necessary the standing orders be so amended as to reflect the following proposal:
Every member of parliament shall, within six months of assuming office and on May 31st of each year thereafter, file with the registrar, the following information, together with such additional information as the registrar may require:
(1)	his or her taxation returns for the year current or preceding;
(2)	his or her financial and pecuniary interests, direct or indirect, of every kind and nature whatsoever, including such interests of the member through his or her spouse and/or dependent children, as well as trusts of which he or she or his or her spouse and/or dependent children are the trustees or beneficiaries.
I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that members will be hard put to find tougher conflict of interest legislation anywhere in the world.
We shall appoint a registrar. Members will be obliged to deposit with him their taxation returns, together with details of their own financial assets and, in addition, those applying to their spouses, children, trustees and beneficiaries. Therefore on the face of it the government will more than meet the requirement referred to in this motion. It will introduce good conflict of interest legislation. True, there are loopholes, and I will not take the time of the House explaining the details. Amendments will be made to

November 20, 1975
Confidence in Government
the Election Expenses Act and conflict of interest guidelines.
I remind the hon. members that the report was unanimous and participated in by members of all parties. In the view of the committee and some observers, it constitutes an outstanding guideline for members and ministers who may find it necessary to avail themselves of the services of the registrar in order to pattern their behaviour in a manner acceptable to their colleagues in the House and to the public as well. Therefore I may disagree with the hon. member for Central Nova about a certain portion of his motion, as I insist that the government will propose an exceptionally good set of guidelines.
Speaking as a member whose riding is involved in one of the topics discussed, I appreciate the hard work of the hon. member for Central Nova and recognize his contribution to the betterment of parliament.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I once knew a Liberal member of parliament whose name I will not mention, he no longer being with us, who, while a potential shareholder or subscriber to a company he sought to have incorporated by act of parliament-the company was subsequently incorporated and he became a shareholder- sat in this House, voted on that company's incorporation, and sat in committee and did the same, because he was privy to information showing that the company was to be awarded a substantial government contract from which he stood to gain much advantage. There is no difference between that situation and the one here, and I think members will agree that it was really wrong for that member of parliament to be so involved.
What really disturbs me is people like the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) rising and complimenting the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) on the integrity with which he spoke and presented his case, while at the same time undercutting him. The hon. member for Lachine (Mr. Blaker) did this too, in a very nice way. I was waiting to hear, for the first time, the allegation of muck raking raised in this debate. And, indeed, it was raised. That is another problem encountered by the opposition when we raise something like this. We encounter scorn, skepticism, and scoffing from members on the government side because those members do not want anything embarrassing to be raised, anything which might muddy the waters.
Our responsibility on this side is very clear, as I see it, and I have had some small experience in raising matters such as this in the past. The event of late 1963 led, in my view, to the publication of the letter of the then prime minister on November 30, 1964, to all his cabinet colleagues, portions of which have been quoted by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker). Yet the caution we have received from the Minister of Transport and the hon. member for Lachine was, in effect: do not take advantage of this privilege which members of parliament are granted to raise matters with immunity in the House knowing we can do so without fear of retribution-I shall have something to say about that in a moment-and because the accused, or whoever is being spoken of in whatever fashion, is not here to defend himself or herself, as the case may be.

There are not many members left in the House, certainly on the other side, who were around in 1963 when these matters were raised and followed up throughout the next year. It may have been a coincidence, but with respect to this possibility of retribution, and opinions which members may express about other members raising matters such as this without proof positive, the belief among members opposite that we over here might, perhaps, raise matters such as this without fear of retribution is quite false.
By way of illustrating this proposition I might say that prior to the event of 1963 in which I was involved, I had occasion to discuss with the then minister of justice a certain case involving two employees of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. After certain matters were raised in the House, matters which were very embarrassing to the government and which caused resignations and, indeed, prosecutions-one person, at any rate, was found guilty of offending against the provisions of the Criminal Code-the full weight of the Government of Canada descended upon those unfortunate employees of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. They were both fired and prosecuted in the courts.
In the Supreme Court, the Supreme Court judge made the remark at that time, with respect to the prosecution of these individuals, that had he himself been in their position he would have done the same thing. But that did not satisfy "the Crown"-I put the word in quotation marks. They pursued the matter through the Court of Appeal on the basis that the judge had applied wrong principles, and were successful in getting a substantial fine imposed on those two civil servants.
What was their crime? Their crime was taking money from one vote intended to be applied for welfare for the Indian people and using it to build houses for Indian people under another vote. That was their crime against the Financial Administration Act. It is true this was not retribution against the individual member of parliament, but it certainly smacks of serious retribution to my mind. I do not have to say more with regard to the caution to be exercised by members on this side in terms of what they might take to be retribution. The wrath of the government did not stop with those two civil servants at that time.
Some 12 years having passed I can speak of these matters now dispassionately. I might say I have not spoken of them to other members of the House in the detail I have now disclosed. However, coincidentally, one might say-I, for one, do not believe it-a short two and a half months after the government had suffered serious embarrassment at my hands involving the resignation of ministers, parliamentary secretaries, and what have you, the full weight of the Department of National Revenue descended upon my shoulders.
Notwithstanding the fact that certain transactions in my business had been fully disclosed to the Director of Taxation in my district, and his approval obtained for these transactions, a re-assessment was made by officials in the Department of National Revenue, coincidentally only two and a half months after the serious embarrassment suffered by the government. The amount involved was the substantial sum of approximately $25,000. The re-assessment was appealed by me and, in substance, the case was won by me before the Tax Appeal Board. But they were not
November 20, 1975

happy to stop there. They meant to nail my hide to the mast, so they tried again, this time not for a mere $25,000; they upped the ante by some $29,000 a few months later.
I wrote to the minister of national revenue at that time suggesting that what was happening was pure harassment because I, as a member of the official opposition, had had the temerity to raise certain matters in 1963, and I stated that unless the harassment ceased I would make the affair public and raise it as a matter of privilege in the House. The minister, I suppose, gave certain directions because the Department of National Revenue called off their dogs and the re-assessment was withdrawn.
That is an illustration of the extent to which the wrath of government can fall on the shoulders of members of the opposition if they have the rashness to raise certain matters in the House. The suggestion of muck-raking or smearing reputations is a very poor device, especially coming from members opposite who may one day-I say just "may"-find themselves on this side of the House, faced with the same kind of duty and responsibility as was so ably carried out today by my hon. friend from Central Nova.
Instead of engaging in the kind of platitudes voiced by the minister today I suggest he could more usefully have used his time by answering the questions which are oustanding on this matter. He suggests there are logical explanations for the granting of the extension of this lease to Sky Shops. A contract which still had four years to run acquired suddenly a five-year extension after it had been in existence for only a year. He told us the reason for this was the need for reconstruction work-there was a space problem and that a rate was to be renegotiated. That strikes me as being very strange, coming from a minister who should know better.
I recall a debate that we had a few years ago on the Prairie Grain Stabilization Act, or some such legislation, where $100 million was being illegally held back from the farmers of this country. A statute specifically spelt out a mandatory responsibility on the minister through whom the Wheat Board reported to distribute those funds as head of the Wheat Board. The minister stood up, this ex-dean of one of the law schools of this country, and tried to convince us that the word "shall" as used in the statute meant that he had some kind of discretion. I could not believe my ears then, and I cannot believe my ears today when the minister says that he believes this is the real reason.
The minister says that members have a responsibility to place before the government all the necessary evidence and information upon which the government can act. That is what I did in 1963, before the matter was raised in the House of Commons, during a discussion of the estimates of the Department of Justice. But nothing was done. Indeed, upon being questioned the government was given the opportunity by the now hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), and I to tell members of the House what the government was going to do about the situation that was then raised. But the government ducked. It pulled the covers over its head, and it was only then that we exposed the whole material.
Confidence in Government
What more does the minister expect from the hon. member for Central Nova, who has provided the minister with documents until they come out of his ears? The minister could not even find certain important information, namely, the liquor contract with the Quebec Liquor Board, so my hon. friend from Central Nova supplied it to him. All the time the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) had a copy of that document in his possession, supplied to him by Mr. Lapointe, one of the principals involved in this what I think is a very sorry and sad mess. How much more disclosure does the minister expect before some action is taken?
Investigations by the RCMP are fine as far as they go, but investigations were undertaken in 1963 by the RCMP. The RCMP followed the course suggested by the Minister of Transport and placed information before the law officers of the Crown, who gave an opinion. The then minister of justice rose in his place and said that their advice was that no criminal offences had been committed; in other words, whitewash it; suppress it if is embarrassing. Subsequently a very distinguished jurist from the province of Quebec differed with the then minister of justice and did in fact find that criminal offences had been committed. I refer to a royal commission specially set up by the government because it was unable to resist the pressure any longer.
The same situation obtains here. The circumstances are such that the matter cries out for a public inquiry. You cannot hide behind the subterfuge of a police investigation carried out by responsible and able police officers, because the truth may not surface if it is politically embarrassing. That is a political fact of life, one of which I have had first-hand experience. It has happened before. If a highly placed official or a government is going to be embarrassed by police investigations, then the police investigation will not see the light of day. This is why the situation cries out for a public inquiry.
I can tell hon. members opposite what the police investigation is going to find. It is going to catch the poor little employee in the Department of Transport who accepted as a gift a pen and pencil set while some guy who makes $95,000 in a few weeks is allowed to get away with a serious conflict of interest. That is not what I understood a very highly respected prime minister of this country to have spelt out in letters to his cabinet colleagues on November 30, 1964. What I understood that prime minister to say was that this kind of conduct was reprehensible and wrong, and that it would not be tolerated by the government.
All we have heard today from the Minister of Transport is excuses. What have we heard from the Senator himself? According to the Globe and Mail for Saturday, November 8, 1975 he said:
What is wrong with having a senator do a little business now and then? Do Canadians expect senators to be drawn from the ranks of the Salvation Army or something?
That is his attitude.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few minutes to read to the House a letter written by the executive secretary to the Prime Minister, Mr. Lalonde, dated April 14, 1970, to Mr. Louis Lapointe of Miron Limitee, 2201 Jarry West, Montreal, Que. This is what he wrote.
My dear Louis:
I acknowledge receipt of your letter dated April 6 as well as the attached documents.
Confidence in Government
I had already seen Mr. Stoner when I received your letter. I had however raised the problem as you had indicated to me during our meeting and in your letter. I asked Mr. Stoner to instruct Mr. Windsor to proceed without delay with this file.
I must say that I am surprised by your refusal to provide a complete copy of your agreement with the Quebec Liquor Board. I cannot accept the principle whereby a public body such as the Quebec Liquor Board may enter into a contract agreement with private concerns and not make public such operation licences. I have no idea what the department will do about your refusal to produce a copy of the agreement, but I must confess that if I were in their place, I would insist to get a copy of the official document. At least I would require a certified copy endorsed by the Board in respect of the extent of your lease.
I hope there will not be undue delays in this matter and if you have any difficulty, be sure to let me know.
Yours very truly,
Marc Lalonde Executive Secretary
Mr. Speaker, I have read this letter into the record to reply to charges made by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) about the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). I believe the whole thing is quite clear, as I indicated before recess. It is a letter of a kind I could have written as a member of parliament.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton could have written such a letter. Indeed, the leader of the opposition could have written it. Those are things we are constantly asked to do by our constituents. I myself do it regularly.
Mr. Speaker, much has been said about the motion presented to the House and which we are debating. Obviously, the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) barked up the wrong tree in this whole thing. He wanted to deal with honesty, integrity and so on in public affairs. He brought up three matters that have been explained by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), namely the dredging contracts, Sky Exports Shop and the Estey inquiry. There are now inquiries of a kind or another and we are awaiting reports.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Central Nova (M. MacKay) evidently lacked seriousness in his accusations. The government is not in the least involved; he has failed to demonstrate that the government had anything to do with this. Whoever reads the hon. member's motion realizes that he is seeking action on the part of the government, that he wants an investigation-indeed he wants an investigation-and that he bases his request on two allegations which the minister has explained, first, the question of the double hearsay, which he admits may be wrong, and second, the question of the return of the tender money, which the minister has said was due on inaccurate and inadmissible tender.
As to the motion itself, the hon. member urges the government to take immediate action to restore public confidence in the government's efforts to control conflict of interest and other improprieties of public officials, most especially with regard to government contract and leasing procedures and practices.
Therefore he is attacking public officials, not the government, not hon. members, but public officials. And what surprises me most is the fact that the hon. member for

November 20, 1975
Confidence in Government
Grenville-Carleton, who is always trying to defend civil servants in the House, is supporting this motion.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, public servants are not here to defend themselves. So, I will try to defend them because those public servants have obligations. First of all, they have guidelines to follow related to their behaviour as individuals confronted with their responsibilities as public servants; second, they have to follow guidelines and regulations set out by each department regarding contracts and the tendering and leasing procedure in general.
Regulation 75-530 dated September 2, 1975 on government dealings sets out all the limitations imposed by every department, and I simply want to quote section 5. The public is not aware of that, since it is believed that the government is free to award the contracts they want whenever they want and to whomever they want to award them. I quote section 5:
5. (1) Subject to this regulation.
(a)	no contract can be agreed on, and
(b)	the amount of a contract cannot be increased without the approval of Treasury Board.
(2) In cases where the present regulations stipulate that the contracting authority is not empowered
(a)	to sign the contract, or
(b)	to increase the amount of the contract, without the approval of the Treasury Board, the latter is authorized to give its approval.
Now, to go back to the instructions. The document was issued by the Treasury Board: "Policies and guidelines for Canadian government contracts". This document contains 41 pages of instructions given to every government department. We readily see what it deals with by consulting the table of contents: first of all, work distribution between the purchasing departments and the common services agencies; the purposes of the document, of which, firstly, the policy. I quote, as follows, from page 5 of that document:
The government purchasing procedure serves the purpose of obtaining supplies and services, of building works and signing leases through contractual provisions which best serve the specific requirements of the programs of the government of Canada. The contracts of the government should be entered into so as to guarantee:
(a)	the best possible terms from the triple point of view of quality, time limits and total cost of the goods or services purchased throughout their useful life;
(b)	a reasonable use of public funds; and
(c)	if needs be, that national policies and objectives are taken into account.
Mr. Speaker, this objective is pursued over 41 pages. There is a section which I regard as very important, the one about the protection of the interests of the Crown, that is of the Canadian people. First, financial guarantees; second, contract arrangements; third, insurances; finally, the purchasing process, the procedure to follow to negotiate contracts between the Crown and individuals in the private sector.
We find a definition of requirements, that is what is needed. There is a list of purchasing methods, or ways of purchasing the goods that are needed. Then the price and the way of determining prices are dealt with. Mr. Speaker, invitations to tender and selection of the contractor are found on page 25 of the document. On that page the procedure to follow to invite tenders is explained.

I quote clause 5.40 on page 25:
5.40	As indicated in the policy statement, the purchasing method used for a given purchase should give eligible businesses the same opportunity to deal with the government, within the application limits. The following guidelines describe different selection methods to be used according to the circumstances.
5.41	Notices in newspapers
5.42	Use of the postal lists of bidders
Mr. Speaker, I shall not read the whole document because it is very long. All I want to indicate by this is that for a long time we have had very strict guidelines on the way the government and civil servants should proceed for awarding contracts. There are restraints as to the duty of civil servants. All I want to indicate in conclusion is that it is impossible, no matter the importance of the guidelines established, to believe that we will be able to obliterate all loopholes and all frauds, human nature being what it is. We try to do away with them as much as possible, but being realistic we realize-
It is impossible, Mr. Speaker, to do away with human nature and criminality. For anyone to think that eventually there will be complete elimination of that conduct is unrealistic.
