Mr. Speaker, I am glad to take part to this opposition day. It has made possible the presentation of a motion relating directly to conflicts of interest. I listened very carefully to the previous speaker who seemed quite intent on defending himself. I do not think that the motion accuses anybody. On the contrary, I think it simply requests Parliament, hon. members, to try to avoid those allusions which have been made for so many years. There were also inquiries that proved the government or governments had certain problems within their departments or services. And when the motion states clearly:
That this House noting the public is concerned-
I think this is ever more important, Mr. Speaker. You and all hon. members are aware that politicians have lost much credibility on account of rumours which are heard now and then. I realize some hon. members may be worried by our present discussions of events which were published in the newspapers. I shall bear testimony to this, shortly. We are not accusing anyone, far from it, but simply avail ourselves of the opportunity to urge the government to scrutinize all its departments and agencies and try to eliminate abuses, if any.
A while ago, the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) admitted that it is not easy to eliminate all wrongdoings. But to which extent should we press the government to check those abuses or those errors-if they are-while profiteers manage to convince the public that politics is a dirty game? In my opinion, this is what we are trying to do when we say that government leaders must be free from any suspicion. I think this is an important requirement that should be met.
November 20, 1975

The newspapers recently reported such cases, which do not improve the standing of members of Parliament. I can read in a newpaper:	"RCMP search Senator Louis
Giguere's offices and home". I am not the one who reports it, the newspapers do; this merely proves how important it is to change the situation and, if necessary, to proceed with a judicial inquiry. I will quote a well known Montreal reporter who believes that such an inquiry should be done. Further, one can read: "RCMP search senator's offices-" This is an excerpt from another Montreal daily newspaper. "RCMP inquire on alleged fraud of $60 million at Mirabel". "Giguere case still on front pages". "$95,000 in assets". "New scandal at Air Canada". This news is reported in the newspapers. A $5,000 bribe to the Liberals.
Mr. Speaker, those are so many newspaper headlines, so many things that lead people to believe that Parliament is definitely corrupt, but I do not think that all those sitting in this Parliament are corrupt.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from an editorial by Claude Ryan who, I believe, is held in high isteem. He refers more specifically to further details provided by a Toronto newspaper The Globe and Mail, concerning the Sky Shop Exports Limited.
Senator Giguere attempted the other evening, before his Senate colleagues, to deny any suspicion of irregularity ... not only did it restrict singularly the full impact of the case ...
Until further notice, any strictly private individual or society is entitled in this country to make gifts to anyone, provided it is done legally. In case of gifts to political parties the Canada Elections Act now requires that they be reported to the returning officer and that this information be made available to the press and the public. But the act was not yet in force at the time of the transactions between Sky Exports Shops and Senator Giguere. Therefore, it could not be involved to blame Mr. Giguere for having bought at unusually attractive conditions in 1972 shares that he was able to sell back a few months later at an incredible profit of almost 2,00.0 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, the title is: "The Giguere Case; Why 2,000 per cent?
Among the other circumstances that look fishy in this story, there are at least three which deserve special attention:
(a) The directors of Sky Exports Shops had at the time a secret guarantee from the Quebec Liquor Board that they would be the only ones allowed to buy alcoholic beverages from the Board for sale at Dorval airport. It is understood that the person at the RAQ responsible for this agreement has been replaced since then. Therefore, there is reason to believe that this type of practice has come to an end. But it is important to know if federal authorities were informed at the time. According to the information made public in the last few days, it seems that they were. How can one explain that they could have been party to a practice which went directly against the rules of free competition for the granting of federal permits?
Well, Mr. Speaker, I think it is indeed something to wonder about. Earlier today, if I remember well, someone mentioned a correspondence between the executive secretary to the Prime Minister, now the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and Mr. Lapointe.
Well, there is no proof in those letters that the minister did something wrong. But the question is there: how come the attitude of the government of Quebec with respect to the granting of those permits was not criticized? A few months after their permit was renewed, the exporters of Sky Exports Shop sold their business at the price of $20 a share, enabling Senator Giguere to make a profit of $95,000 within a year. Considering most of the value of that busi-
Confidence in Government
ness lay in the exclusive permit it was granted by the federal government, he made quite a pretty penny indeed.
Well, representations were made to the executive secretary to the Prime Minister, now Minister of National Health and Welfare, by the chairman of Sky Exports Shop who asked him to appeal to the Minister of Transport to speed up the expected decision. The present Minister of National Health and Welfare denies receiving any monies in that respect, and we will take his word on it.
However, in his letter to the Deputy Minister of Transport, we note an apparently unusual insistance. Here is, Mr. Speaker, an editorial of a very well known daily Montreal paper which raises a number of questions and calls for answers. I think it is quite normal and in the interest of the public right that we should ask certain questions to which the public is entitled to expect answers. Earlier today, I think, someone mentioned $10,000 paid to Mr. Lapointe to have him come a few times to Ottawa, and request an extension of his contracts.
It might be important to know up to what point the government should not disclose that $10,000 expense. It does not take $10,000 indeed, Mr. Speaker, to come three or four times to Ottawa. I think agreement to that extension was obtained within one month, from January 8 to February or March.
Mr. Lapointe, I agree, made a few trips to Ottawa. He was given $2,000, $3,000 or $5,000 to negotiate, hoping there would be an affirmative response. How was that $10,000 spend? Those are questions we ask without accusing anyone, but I think the public would be quite interested in knowing where that money went and whether Mr. Lapointe really spend $10,000 on trips and meals. We have nothing against that, we would like the question to be asked, considering the amount, to come from time to time to solicit a little service for reasons we do not know either.
In any case, I think it is a question that deserves to be asked. As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, the motion before us today invites members to ask the government for closer monitoring that we have had up to now, and particularly eliminate those scandals we have across the country. We had others, with the result that the public loses faith in men in public life, the credibility not only of this government but of this Parliament-and we make up this Parliament- is also down. It is not very interesting for us to be catalogued in a general way because newspapers indeed report suppositions perhaps, as well as allegations, and in certain cases evidence was put forward.
So, that is why we try to bring this government to shed light on matters such as those with which I dealt earlier, and which are publicly reported in newspapers, and I think nobody can blame us for working in that sense. I heard other members make certain comments today in that respect and we are trying to get rid of and eliminate those conflicts of interest. Obviously, the leaders of a government must be above suspicion. The kind of intolerable situation which undermines public confidence in the normal process of our institutions in equally important.
We would hope to bring about such things. All these articles and statements encourage many people to make easy and negative criticisms about politicians, and we are always disappointed to see such articles or scandals,

November 20, 1975
Confidence in Government
because we are directly involved, whether we want it or not. We must ensure that politicians exercise great care regarding conflicts of interest. A piece of legislation was adopted hardly a year ago on this matter, and I believe that we can never do too much to eliminate these conflicts of interest. I recognize that people in public life must, and rightly so, be careful about public morality, and this gives us even more reason to demand stricter control on the part of the government. It is up to the government to throw some light and clarify any such matters which might raise some doubts about the honesty of politicians. Once again, I believe that we are justified in demanding that these things reported in the newspapers be clarified. Reporters have brought these things up and the public is expecting some answers. It is therefore important to clarify the relationship that may exist between the government and certain financial interests.
Mr. Speaker, such is the purpose of this motion and we are asking only one thing from the government: That it throw light on some points which are now unclear-and the public is aware that there have been quite attractive profits. Are these profits justified? We should be told if they are. We have nothing against the fact that an amount of $10,000 was granted to a gentleman who has some representations to make, as long as these things make sense. Those are the questions that we are asking. Men who may not have been directly involved with a department, as they now are, may have had relationships which are quite legitimate in politics, and we admit this. But once again, we are asking the government to clarify those things that we and the population find fishy and which were brought to the attention of the public. In the light of the information we might get on these matters, it is possible that the answer be accurate. And if errors were made, we will have to ask the government to take action. A judicial inquiry has been urged. A well known editorialist among many other people feels there is ground for an inquiry. I believe the government will never have been served better than by the group of members urging that the matter be aired. These members would be happy to see the government put a stop to those practices, that corruption the public is so concerned about. I believe it is in Parliament's interest and it is important to both members in this House and those who wish to enter prolitics that they should not be termed generally "shady politicians". I therefore hope the government will shed light on those things and what it will be capable of preventing their future occurrence.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us, urging the government to take action "to restore confidence in the government's efforts to control conflict of interest and other improprieties of public officials," is timely, but limited and limiting in that it seems to place on government alone a responsibility that should properly be shared by the opposition, the civil service, by the media, and by all Canadians who care about the democratic process.
Present day concern about the conduct of public officials reflects a number of factors-some positive, some less so. On the positive side, public awareness and public requirements of standards of behaviour from elected officials and

civil servants are higher than they have ever been. Practices which were tolerated ten years ago, such as, for example, establishing private trust funds to supplement a politician's income are no longer acceptable.
We must all welcome this greater vigilance of the public and the clearly articulated wish of Canadians that politicians not only be, but appear to be independent and not subject to inappropriate influence or an appearance of influence in the exercise of their public duties and responsibilities.
The Election Expenses Act, with its provisions for disclosure and its encouragement by way of tax credits of small donations, represents one important response of the government to this legitimate concern of Canadians.
The green paper entitled "Members of Parliament and Conflict of Interest" which was prepared in July, 1973, under the auspices of the Privy Council, represents another government initiative to remain responsive to the contemporary needs and values of Canadians.
The then president of the privy council recognized that:
... the evolution of public standards has out-distanced the development of formal rules which should apply to the conduct of members of parliament. Furthermore, the role of the member of parliament has become more complex and members may increasingly find themselves in situations for which no adequate rules or guidelines exist to aid them in ensuring that their conduct respects their fiduciary duty. Perhaps most important, the increasing involvement of modern government in society has blurred the line between public and private matters to the extent that both the public and parliament seem agreed that a systematic and public set of standards is now required.
Although the proposals made in the green paper were restricted in their application to members of the House of Commons and senators, the green paper stated that the government intended to develop "a comprehensive policy on the standard of conduct expected of officials at all levels of government.
On December 18, 1973, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) tabled an order in council setting out guidelines for public servants and those appointed to public office by the Governor General in Council. The underlying principle of these guidelines is an obligation on the part of public servants to act in a manner so scrupulous that it will bear the closest public scrutiny. Public servants are, therefore, required not to place themselves in a position where they are under obligation to any person who might benefit from special consideration or favour on their part, or seek in any way to gain special treatment from them. Equally, a public servant may not have a pecuniary interest that could conflict in any manner with the discharge of his official duties.
Public servants are now expected, as are ministers of the Crown, upon appointment to office, to disclose all business interests that could be construed as being in actual or potential conflict with their official duties, and to arrange their private affairs in a manner that will prevent conflicts of interest from arising if there is any risk of that occurring. Public servants are required to manage their affairs so as not to benefit, or appear to benefit, from the use of information acquired in the course of their official duties that is not generally available to the public.
In the matter of contracts specifically mentioned in the motion of the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), public servants are asked not to place them-
November 20, 1975

selves in a position where they could derive any direct or indirect benefit or interest from a government contract over which they can influence decisions.
In the past the matter of conflict of interest with regard to public servants was not of great public concern. It was a matter of principle that on entering the public service one severed all connections with the business world and with political parties. However, in recent years new policies in the public service have brought some changes. For example, under the Public Service Commission's career assignment program business people have been brought into the service, and public servants have been assigned to jobs in industry. In the senior executive interchange program public service appointments are filled by businessmen and women, and public servants are transferred to industry on a temporary basis. Deputy ministers have also been brought in from outside the public service.
In these new circumstances men and women may find themselves in situations where their public duty conflicts with their own interests or those of the company with which they have been associated. On the other hand one can argue that an official who withdraws from decision making in matters relating to his or her former business may well become ineffective in his or her public service capacity.
When the Prime Minister tabled these guidelines, Crown corporations were also asked to develop standards and guidelines for their employees. The then minister of justice was requested to review existing legislation with respect to judicial or quasi-judicial appointments, with a view to bringing it into conformity with established standard^ of conduct for other officials in government service. On December 31, 1973, the Treasury Board followed the Prime Minister's directive by issuing a circular to all heads of departments. The initial disclosures were to be made by June 30, 1974.
During the debate on the guidelines the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) raised the criticism that the order in council lacked definitions and provisions for enforcement.
In the case of members of parliament a number of statutes now contain provisions on conflict of interest. These include the Canada Elections Act, the Criminal Code, the House of Commons Act, the Senate and House of Commons Act, the Rules of the Senate, and the Laws and Usages of the Parliament of the United Kingdom, as preserved by Section 18 of the British North America Act and Section 4 of the Senate and the House of Commons Act.
Part III of the green paper dealt with possible weaknesses, omissions, and loopholes in current legislation, and considered that some provisions may be out of date and in need of revision in the light of changing circumstances. The green paper proposed that legislative provisions concerning conflicts of interest of members of parliament should be contained in a new act to be known as the Independence of Parliament Act, with the exception of bribery which would continue to be dealt with under the Criminal Code.
At present Canadian legislation on government contracts held by members of the House of Commons is found
Confidence in Government
almost entirely in the Senate and House of Commons Act. The basic principle expressed is that a member of the House of Commons or candidate should not be party to a government contract as a result of which he, or she, is a recipient of public funds. This provision has been criticized on grounds of ambiguousness.
The discussion draft of the Independence of Parliament Act, which was included as an appendix to the green paper, made seven proposals with regard to government contracts. The principle, generally, is that participation in a government contract by a member of parliament constitutes a conflict of interest and a violation of the member's fiduciary duty. It was also recommended that no member of parliament should be permitted to participate in the management or direction of a company having a government contract or agreement. It was also suggested that disclosure should be made by registering annually a list of companies in which the member was an officer, director or manager.
Some of the exceptions proposed were: that a member of parliament should be permitted to own shares in publicly traded companies that deal with the government, provided the member is not a director, nor in active management of those companies, and that he or she holds less than 5 per cent of the stock, such interest to be registered annually; that a member may participate in a contract if the aggregate value is less than $1,000 in any one fiscal year, the details of such interest also to be registered; that a member may hold a government contract if the completion of such contract devolves on him by descent, marriage, or operation of law, provided the member disposes of the contract within 12 months. Again the details are to be registered.
The discussion draft proposed that the former tenuous custom of declaring financial interests in a matter during debate and question period should be formalized and incorporated in the Standing Orders of the House and Rules of the Senate. No particular sanction was proposed for a violation, although a wide variety of sanctions is available. It was suggested that the standing committees of both Houses would provide guidance regarding particular situations.
The draft suggested retention of the practice whereby a member of the House, or a senator, is prohibited from voting on any question in which he or she has a pecuniary interest. It was proposed that the Standing Orders of the House and Rules of the Senate should caution members to exercise care in managing their investments so that they do not benefit, or appear to benefit, from the use of information which may have been available to them confidentially. Severe penalties were suggested for breaches.
As hon. members know, the green paper was referred first to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, which has reported to this House. The Senate is currently discussing the report. The green paper was intended as a first step in the evolution of a systematic and public set of standards. I hope that today's discussion, together with the report of the Committee on Privileges and Elections, and the debate in the Senate will contribute to this process.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) expressed concern about the green paper being still before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

November 20, 1975
Confidence in Government
Apparently he did not know that the committee reported last June. During the proceedings of that committee the same sense of urgency was not always demonstrated by his colleagues.
At early committee meetings some opposition members wanted public disclosure and severe restrictions for ministers only. Being newly elected I was surprised to hear opposition members suggest that private members of parliament could not be in conflict of interest. Some opposition members preferred to use their time questioning the authorship of the green paper instead of discussing the content or proposing new measures. Despite these initial delays all parties worked constructively on the guidelines which, as the hon. member for Lachine-Lakeshore (Mr. Blaker) said this afternoon, went beyond the green paper's recommendations and were accepted unanimously.
As the green paper stated, "the prestige and effectiveness of the Canadian parliament depend greatly on the public's confidence in the willingness of parliamentarians to resolve conflicts of interest." You will note that the reference is to parliament and parliamentarians, not to government alone. The motion before the House deals with the restoration of public confidence. Just as the green paper deals with avoiding not only conflict of interest but the appearance of conflict of interest, I take it it is the duty of parliamentarians not only to define and observe rules of conduct but also to inform the public of the existence of those rules, and thus maintain public confidence.
Members of the official opposition have a special responsibility to be accurate as well as hard hitting in their criticisms-to present a balanced picture of things as they are, not to attribute bad motives or behaviour without proof. A well respected member of the official opposition once said at a meeting of the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections that democracy is a delicate flower. Certainly the number of healthy democracies in the world today is disconcertingly small, and we cannot take ours for granted.
Free speech, open criticism, and discussion of issues are central to democracy, but negative cynical criticism and attacks on personal integrity tend to erode public confidence in democratic institutions. Maintaining and restoring public confidence require leadership by government, but also require restraint and concern for accuracy on the part of both opposition and the media.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what we have before us today is a gently worded resolution by the quiet and gentle member from Central Nova, containing the word improprieties, and suggesting the government should take immediate action to restore public confidence. He then goes on to give one or two bits of evidence.
I want to say at the outset that the samples of evidence given in the motion are such a small proportion of the sins of the government that you hardly even know there is more than a mosquito biting an elephant. And in all the answers we have heard from the government today not one has even mentioned that $95,000. The minister made reference to picayune little points made by the hon. member for

Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). Everyone knows what we are talking about, and they carefully avoid it.
Let me just list the type of things which should be in the motion, Mr. Speaker, and I could double it and triple it if I wished. How about the dismissal of the Chief Commissioner of the Board of Grain Commissioners for only one cause-he refused to play the political patronage game of the government in Montreal?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, how about the fact that at this very moment there are criminal court proceedings going on in Regina, Saskatchewan-the chief operational head of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has had his preliminary hearing and faces criminal fraud proceedings? And we get these moral lectures on behaviour as it should be, according to some mythical guidelines. The government, instead of trying to bring this out into the open, periodically tries to bring the Prairie Farm Assistance Act here to be repealed so we will not be able to talk about it any more.
All hon. members remember just a short while ago that one newspaper which took a different editorial position from the one the government has, lost all its government advertising. Who enforced this action? Why, it was the then minister of energy, mines and resources. Punish a person, if he disagrees with the government! This is not ten years ago in the weak days of government under Pearson. This is right now. And what did they do with that minister? They made him the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). They have the morality of a bunch of alley cats.
Look at the questions about the Montreal pipeline I put a year ago in the House. Who was on this committee representing the government dealing with the business firms and trying to get them to build the Montreal pipeline? First, I heard they were to get the Deputy Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson). Then the Energy Board officers were there. Finally, after a little bit of questioning, the minister admitted that someone from his department was there. From his office, is what he meant to say. And one of the reasons for the delay was somebody telling these companies that if they wanted things speeded up they should make sure they hired public engineering people from the right place. The minister in this case was the same minister of energy, mines and resources, the patronage boss for the province of Ontario.
If I dipped my nose into the smell which comes out of CIDA it would be a stinking mess you would have to bring into this House. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) made a trip to Israel. Did he use a government plane, a commercial plane? Oh, no. He made the trip on a friend's plane-a friend who was doing big business with the government.
Then we have the great mystery of what we will call the Austin case. The member for Central Nova tried to get several questions placed on the order paper. They were not allowed on the order paper. These questions were addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). They have been published in the newspapers but are not allowed in this House. Is the government trying to build up confidence in the minds of the people of Canada that it is running a clean shop here?
November 20, 1975

I will go further, Mr. Speaker. Even with the Elections Act of 1974 in place there is blackmail going on with the business and professional men in this country undertaken by the bagmen of the government. These are the types of thing which should be in the motion and I think the hon. member for Central Nova should be criticized because he is so moderate, and so gentle with regard to these very serious things.
Last evening I spent a little time reading through some of the recommendations of the five volumes of the Glassco Commission Report. This was a commission set up 15 years ago to try to tighten up the looseness and the duplication in government spending about which the member for Central Nova was talking. All I wish to say is that the royal commission reported some 12 years ago, recommending that we decentralize the control of this huge labyrinth of administration from Treasury Board and put responsibility on the individual departments to do more. Then it adds these phrases, over and over again, "Pay these civil servants more so they can do the job more effectively, and then insist on accountability." What they have done is raise the salaries all right. They have not decentralized it very much, and they forgot the key word, accountability.
What do I mean by accountability? When these sort of things happen to a person in charge at a responsible level, a member of this parliament, whether senator or member of this House, you ask him to resign. That is accountability. Anyone having anything to do with these sort of smelly operations should resign. Or you tell senior civil servants, who are now paid the equivalent of the salaries of corporate heads, that they are fired, without any recommendation for another job.
In this particular case we have the ex-minister of transport, the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson), and if the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) wants to prove to the people of this country that this thing will never happen again, he should ask the minister for his resignation, because he presided over the treasury board, I understand, when this decision was made. Ask the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), who was working then for the Prime Minister and, according to the evidence, doing a constituency job as a friend of a man from Montreal. He gave an order that the file should be opened and acted on. I ask for that minister's resignation. Then the people will know you are taking action to stop this type of thing.
Patronage is not a new word in this House. I do not suppose that even in an NDP government you get rid of it. Even they are hiring defeated politicians. But there has to be a certain standard, or a politician loses credibility across the country. I happen to come from the province of Saskatchewan where we endured for many decades the machine politics of the Liberals, euphemistically called the Gardiner machine, but it kept on going after he disappeared.
I belonged to an administration that was here from 1957 to 1963, and many senior newsmen in the press gallery today claim that we defeated ourselves by trying to stop patronage and corruption in places like the post office, public works, PFRA and PFAA. Not one of the people
Confidence in Government
involved was fired. When the 2,000 people that I had personal knowledge of were told there would be no dismissals but to keep out of this silly political business, only six broke that direction from the minister, and not one of those six was fired. They got a second warning and then were removed.
The day of hiring people for their political wallop, the day of using civil servants to act at election time, is over except for the west. The present political czar in the west- I call him the crown prince-is trying to rebuild the organization, and this explains why the Liberals ran third in so many districts in Saskatchewan last June. In the minister's own area the Liberals ran a poor third. I am simply pointing out that we have heard a lot of nonsense in this debate from hon. members opposite. No one has even mentioned the $95,000 which is evidence that infringes the members of parliament act and the members of the senate act. This absence of any mention of the $95,000 means that ministers are not enforcing accountability among their own people. As the Prime Minister said the other day, he could not see any evidence of conflict of interest in the payment of $95,000 just for being a friend.

speechtext: He never said that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Nipissing reminds me of a rain barrel; the emptier the barrel, the more noise it makes when you beat it. He was certainly making a noise tonight. I know the tricks of these country people. When they have a poor case they yell at the top of their voice. The hon. member mentioned, for example, that he was not here when all these ministers were going right and left while the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) was on the warpath. Nearly a score of ministers disappeared from that one administration over a period of time. The hon. member reminds me of what I told the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) some time ago, that you rarely find a good kernel of wheat in a full barrel of rat manure. Translated that means that if you keep associating with these people you become one of them.
What this whole matter adds up to is that in the last two decades we have moved into a permissive society. What started out as a move to get the government out of the bedroom has spread all through government, but instead of sex what we are talking about is a new form of permissiveness-that it is all right to put bagmen in the Senate. It is all right for them to make representations to friends, or to get friends to make representations to them. It is all right to appoint friends to high positions in Air Canada. It is all right to appoint defeated politicians to jobs across the country. There is nothing the matter with appointing a well trained, able, defeated politician. But when all of them are given an appointment, questions arise.
What we are witnessing in typical Canadian fashion is a Watergate-Canadian style. As the hon. member for Gren-ville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) pointed out this afternoon, when the Minister of Transport, an ex-professor of law and ex-minister of justice, stood up in the House and made his unctuous, sanctimonious speech, it sounded so much like the repeated disclaimers of ex-president Nixon-everything will be disclosed, everything is all right-that type of

November 20, 1975
Confidence in Government
attitude proves to me and convinces me that there is a deliberate policy here of putting the lid on disclosure.
I mentioned the Board of Grain Commissioners. We do not have to go out and get a witness; the witness is sitting in the House today as a member of parliament. I refer to the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) who was chief commissioner of the Board of Grain Commissioners, and was fired by the government. Under pressure he refused to play politics with the movement of grain to the hungry people of the world, and the answer was dismissal. I am the one who said that the best thing to do when this sort of thing happens is to run for office, become a member of parliament, and whenever you have the occasion just remind the government of the type of people they are.
I mentioned the PFAA charges. I am not going to say anything about the particular charges because they are still before the court at the present time, but I am not going to hide my intentions. When the court cases are over, that will not be the end of the matter. In a court, tangible evidence has to be produced. If anyone is going to suggest to the rational people of this country that one man at a level way down designed this whole operation, that will not be acceptable to the House of Commons. We want to know how far this conspiracy to spend public money for purposes of electing government members reached into the parliamentary secretaryships, the executive assistants, and perhaps even members of the cabinet. Those are not questions you turn over to the police for investigation. This is a responsibility of the Committee on Privileges and Elections, and I am glad that the hon. member for Lachine-Lakeshore stood up today and said that was the place for them, because we will be there before this thing is over.
As I conclude I want to remind hon. members on the other side of the House that these dismissals I recommend are not only for ministers but for one or two civil servants right at the upper end. Once you cut the knot and get rid of them, it is amazing to find how few there really are.
Just to show how serious this is, let me put it this way. The great strength of the Canadian civil service over the years has been in the fact that they watch the politicians and they hold on to their integrity. Remember the civil servant in the deputy minister's office a few years ago when the political manoeuverers around here were trying to get an immigrant in who was offering big sums of money for Canadian citizenship. This deputy minister stood in their way, and said no. I would like to believe that he is still there, but he is not. The truth is astounding, because there was a deputy minister in Energy, Mines and Resources last year who jumped to principal clerk in the Prime Minister's office, and six months later seven senior civil servants decided to retire. That is how serious this is.
What we have to do here is ask the Prime Minister for action, and my interpretation of action in this motion is the dismissal of all those associated with this case as a warning to all those others doing this monkeyshining that they had better run for the hills.
Today is November 20, the birthday of Sir Wilfrid Lauri-er. In the interest of getting back the confidence of the people the government should indicate its intention to stop

this kind of monkeyshines by making this day in 1975 known as the Laurier day massacre of all those people sliding in and out, and doing these things.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my contribution to this debate will deal with a problem that is not only a dilemma with which the government is faced but involves a situation which has become quite intolerable as it affects not only every citizen of our country, but every aspect of their every day lives.
I want to take a rational and responsible approach by identifying the issue for debate today as a human problem. It is a human weakness to be arrogant when in a safe position of power. It is human to be loyal to one's friends who have helped and offered support along the rugged trail of political success. To fall and succumb to the dangers of such human activities is not only the weakness of the present government but, indeed, it is a weakness of our political process or system.
It is, of course, also human to try to secure one's position, and to strive for bigger and better things. Regardless of how hard we try to regulate and control the lives of individuals, we will never succeed in making everyone equal by destroying the competitive spirit in individuals and the desire to be at least equal or, ideally, just a nose length ahead of the next guy.
The politician in that sense is no different from the businessman. The latter struggles to become established, celebrates the official opening of his first plant as the achievement of a lifetime, and as soon as the first customer walks through the door and the first day's proceeds are counted, the process of expansion begins. The businessman, like the politician, must, in order to secure his position, broaden his support, expand his scope, diversify his operations, and make himself indispensable.
We hear much about powerful groups within our society today, such as large corporations which have evolved from the world of business and have become so powerful, monopolistic, and indispensable in nature that they now pose the most serious threat to the survival of the very system from which they evolved-the free enterprise world.
There are large unions too which, in order to secure their position to offer more and better concessions to their members, have made themselves indispensable and all-powerful, even ready now to challenge the institution itself.
The institution of government was planned and built with regard to these weaknesses, and in normal times the safeguards are sufficient. Unlike the businessman, the politician must expose himself to the test periodically. The government itself is subjected to scrutiny by the House of Commons in normal times. The collective work of this Chamber is exposed to sober, second look and evaluation by elders who have mastered the art of life and who have, by virtue of their accomplishments, been appointed to serve our country, if for no other purpose than to assure that the politicians who bear on their shoulders such great responsibility do not allow these human weaknesses to influence their work or their decisions.
November 20, 1975

I said that this was so during normal times. However, we are not living in normal times. Something has gone wrong with the traditional process. Somehow a very powerful and very determined group of people have been able to free themselves of the constraints of the democratic system and are ruling instead of governing. They are possessed by yet another human weakness, namely, greed. Those who belong to this group have become the masters not the servants of their constituents. They have joined in unholy matrimony with the other powerful groups that have helped them on their way.
To be appointed to the Senate today means also to be offered directorships in a series of corporate offices. To be appointed to the executive council means to receive contributions to the election campaign from the unions.
How did this all come about? Many of us have speculated about this and have reached different conclusions. Money is power, or it provides an effective means of controlling power. There is no better way to demonstrate the centralization of power which we have experienced in Canada than by examining the fiscal and monetary strategy of the government.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is right, of course, as is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), when he says that the increase in government spending does not fairly reflect the activities and the increase in public services since, as they both argue, the increase in their budget from $6 billion to $32 billion in just ten years is mostly due to transfers of funds-taking from the rich and giving to the poor, taking from certain provinces and giving to other provinces.
The fact is that today almost all disposable income from our gross national product is fed into a central hopper. The super group of which I have spoken thus assumes the right to redistribute this seemingly unlimited wealth in a way not necessarily in the interests of the country as a whole. Is it then, having regard to the human weaknesses I have spoken of, any wonder that there are some Canadians who have been identified as friends of this all-powerful group and have become very rich and powerful themselves?
I want to take a closer look at some of those people behind the scenes. Some have already been identified by my colleagues. Once close to the top they become one and the same person. Their activity and influence is not confined to just the Ministry of Transport, the Ministry of Public Works, or the Ministry of Supply and Services.
I said earlier that the actions of these barons affect every aspect of the lives of Canadians. In the interest of continuity of the story my colleagues have laid out before us, let me lay out another story. Let us take a closer look at yet another most dedicated public servant who at the present time fulfils the role in the Prime Minister's office which was formerly carried out by, in Mr. Lapointe's most affectionate words, "my dear friend Marc". While a westerner of dubious distinction, who has now gone to his reward, filled the position for a brief period of time, the job is now in the hands of a most distinguished servant of the public interest, namely, Mr. James Coutts.
Mr. Coutts' career is colourful, and like his predecessors he too has of course friends who call him by his first name.
Confidence in Government
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Coutts also has friends who are close enough to him to make certain of his actions justifiable. He was once an appointment secretary of the former and late Prime Minister Pearson. Like so many of the people on the monopoly board of Liberal players, he retired early to assume a career of consulting. He became one of that elite group of Canadians who divide amongst themselves every year about $1 billion.
He became affiliated with the firm of Canada Consulting of Toronto, a firm which over the years enjoyed quite an impressive array of public assignments. He took some time out in 1974 to manage the affairs of our Prime Minister during those years. Madam Speaker, I could not possibly give you a complete list of that firm's success stories about which I am speaking. I refer to Canada Consulting of Toronto. But there is one insignificant little assignment which fits into my story best. It was the assignment to find a new head for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The former president was being retired, and the position had to be filled. It was not a difficult task, even though the price tag was, I understand, in the tens of thousands of dollars.
Three names were suggested. The choice was not difficult. Mr. William Teron was the obvious choice, a man with a most distinguished career in the field of housing, particularly high cost housing, because this is what we have much of in our country and are to be assured of more in the future.
Mr. Teron swiftly reciprocated. The corporation had to be restructured to make room for the technocrats who fit better into the scheme of things. Yes, Madam Speaker, as you might have guessed Mr. Coutts got the contract to recommend the changes which would bring peace and tranquility to the corporation. This assignment, I am told, was in the six figure dollar league, indeed a just reward.
Now, Madam Speaker, the new president of the corporation is endowed with a good measure of the human qualities of which I have talked earlier. He is on his way to making himself indispensable. He had little time for the former minister, and less time for the present housing minister. He has recently assumed the responsibility of the top civil service position in the Ministry of Urban Affairs.
He has been known to have the Secretary of the Privy Council write his public statements for him. He is now in a position to make, as well as carry out, the government's housing policy. The same efficiency experts who are the fear of the Housing Corporation are now also extending their activities to the Urban Affairs department. I am sure all will soon be in order there as well. But, while the enforcers of Canada Consulting are still roaming the halls of high government places, Mr. Coutts himself has moved back to a position from where he can serve his country, but more important serve his friends and those of the Liberal Party more diligently and effectively.
As you already know, he is now the principal secretary of the Prime Minister, and one wonders how many privileged Canadians feel, by virtue of their friendship with Mr. Coutts, justified to demand his services. But let us go back to our friend Mr. Teron, and let us bring into focus a short profile of his private business career. Time will only permit us to touch on the highlights of his most recent background.

November 20, 1975
Confidence in Government
In 1966 Mr. Teron, with a number of interesting people, incorporated a company called MNS Investment Limited. Along with Mr. Paul Matheson and J. B. Whitely we see names such as Paul Martin, Sr., Jack Austin, and Maurice Strong. These are very familiar names. Maurice Strong is known to us through his close relationship with the former secretary of state for external affairs and now our High Commissioner to England, who appointed Mr. Strong to oversee Canada's efforts in the field of foreign aid. Mr. Strong has lately been seen walking around carrying a Petro-Can.
In February of 1967 Etron Ltd. was incorporated to manage, I understand, the real estate properties Mr. Teron had accumulated. Messrs. Snipper, Cohen and Murray were the solicitors who incorporated the company and maintained the company's office. One of these gentlemen earned Mr. Teron's blind trust in recognition of his services.
Next we see Canadian Interurban Properties, a subsidiary of Power Corporation, acquire the assets of a company called William Teron Limited. He becomes vice-president in charge of planning and development for Interurban Properties. Plan and develop he did.
A short and unhappy corporate relationship with Cam-peau Corporation proved not too lucrative for Mr. Teron. We see him forming a new company called William Teron and Associates. This company concentrated on building apartments, hotels, and office buildings in large urban areas. Next we see the formation of a company called St. Maurice Capital Corporation. This group in 1970 acquired the outstanding shares of MNS Investments. The MNS shareholders, of course, gained an interest in the new company. Incidentally, among the investments held at the time or re-organization was about $55,000 worth of Brame-da Resources, and we also know all about that company.
It was around that time, or by late 1970, that Mr. Teron was seen to spend much time in the office of the then housing minister. Mr. Hignetts' terms as president of CMHC was due to expire in June of 1971, but was extended for two years after much backroom activity. This provided Mr. Teron with time to round out his empire and prepare his blind trust.
Other corporate names appear to complete the web. General Mortgage Corporation is taken over by St. Maurice Capital, and St. Maurice Properties becomes another subsidiary. And then, of course, there is the firm which maintains a penthouse office suite in the Carleton Towers, and which evolved from Etron Limited early in 1974. An impressive list of friends have found refuge there.
One does not have to step off the property surrounding this building to admire the real estate empire of that select group of great Canadians. Madam Speaker, one could go on and on. The question, of course, we have to ask ourselves is, how was it possible for Mr. Teron, who became president of CMHC in 1973, to divest himself of his friends and business interests? The answer, of course, is that it is not possible. CMHC, of course, depends on many of these corporations I have mentioned as a delivery system for the national housing program. His holdings are in blind trust, and that is all that is needed to conform with the 1973 conflict of interest guidelines behind which the Prime

Minister seeks refuge every time an embarrassing question is asked.
Blind trust to people like Mr. Teron means that Canadians have to blindly trust that the friends of the Liberal Party are acting not in their own interest, but in the interest of our country. If one examines the financial reports of the many and varied interests Mr. Teron held before and after assuming control of these high public offices, one comes to the conclusion that either Mr. Teron was managing his interests poorly before, or that his powerful position has something to do with the healthy growth of some of these companies after he blindly entrusted the management to someone else. In either case, this gentleman's qualifications are in question.
I want to quote from the 1973 guidelines which govern the conduct of public servants in such high offices. My colleagues have touched on the guidelines for government and members of parliament. I should like to quote three or four paragraphs:
3.	No conflict should exist or appear to exist between the private interests of public servants and their official duties. Upon appointment to office, public servants are expected to arrange their private affairs in a manner that will prevent conflicts of interest from arising.
4.	Public servants should exercise care in the management of their private affairs so as not to benefit, or appear to benefit, from the use of information acquired during the course of their official duties, which information is not generally available to the public.
5.	Public servants should not place themselves in a position where they could derive any direct or indirect benefit or interest from any government contracts over which they can influence decisions ...
8. Public servants should not accord, in the performance of their official duties, preferential treatment to relatives or friends or to organizations in which they or their relatives of friends have an interest, financial or otherwise.
Well, Madam Speaker, we will let you and the Canadian people judge in Mr. Teron's case.
I have only been able, in the short time allotted to me, to make passing reference to the activities of just one of many small groups of people who, in my opinion, are ripping off the system. I wish it were possible to demonstrate to the House how the activities of these powerful players in the Liberal monopoly game affect interest rates for domestic living in Canada-surely one of the most serious problems contributing to the high cost of housing. But time does not permit.
Let me rather pose this question, Madam Speaker: where is it all going to end? Well, times are changing. We do not enjoy the same degree of financial success and prosperity that we experienced in the post-war period. The gap between rich and poor is widening, and Canadians are about to take a closer look at those who shape the destiny of our country. What they will see is not a pretty picture, and they will demand a change.
Then there are people like Walter Rudnicki, a long time dedicated civil servant who fell victim to their frightening power play, and who will not surrender without a fight. His tragic case is before the courts, and he will not compromise is rights as a Canadian for a settlement out of court.
As I have said during my opening remarks, none of us are immune to these human weaknesses. What is going on in Canada today is only a result of the indifference and
November 20, 1975

ignorance of too many Canadians who have kept this government in power for too long and have allowed it to circumvent the democratic process.
I know that there are those of our colleagues, some of whom even sit on the other side of the House, who are not of the privileged few who head their letters "My Dear Marc", or "My Dear Jim", who will help us to bring the era to an end. Let us hope it will not be too late.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis Fox (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank my dear colleague from Calgary. I was thinking about his remarkable comments on the results of a certain game.
Madam Speaker, I now come to the subject of this debate. Points have been raised, arguments have been made during the day by members of the official opposition. I would simply like to say that we had the impression today of witnessing a "de-escalation". On the basis of insinuations which seem serious by themselves, supported by anonymous affidavits which were flourished in the air, all that resulted during the debate in the colleagues of the mover of the motion themselves taking a stance against him. We witnessed a real "de-escalation", as I said. His own colleagues seemed very embarrassed to come back to the subject he had himself raised, and during the afternoon we heard apologies, people almost apologizing for being associated with the kind of things done today by the member in question.
The hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) for example is maintaining that no accusations are being made. These are the hon. member's words. The hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) complains that the motion is incomplete. Well, if he has criticism to make about the incompetence of those who drafted the motion, he only has to turn around and face his own colleagues. Indeed he was really successful in underlining the incompetence of his colleagues who drafted the motion. It was almost an election speech, possibly unveiling his own election campaign and I hope, Madam Speaker, that it will be cleaner than the speech he made this evening.
It looks as if he chose the anniversary of Laurier to start off. He spoke of a slaughter. I have the impression, Madam Speaker, that the blue slaughter of February will be a reality well before his pious wishes for the red slaughter. He criticized my colleague the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) because he was not here in 1963 and because he does not know the great debates they may have had in this House at that time.
Madam Speaker, if the spectacle the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain gave us tonight is typical of the type of debate, of things that went on in the House of Commons at that time, I am very happy to be among the colleagues of the hon. member for Nipissing rather than those of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain.
And so, we had a "de-escalation" throughout the day. The hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) started off, followed by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) who felt obliged to excuse him by saying it was the role of
Confidence in Government
the opposition to make that type of accusation. The hon. member for Joliette, as I mentioned before, also said that in fact the accusations were not made against the government, that they were pious wishes because everyone is interested in improving public administration in Canada. The situation is quite embarrassing. The last speaker of the party, the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) did not even speak to the motion before the House. The only thing he mentioned was a series of "Dear Jim" and "Cher Marc", making allusions to people in the office of the Prime Minister, and more particularly to the current head of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. And those very same people, on the back and front benches of that opp party, Madam Speaker, keep saying to the government that more people in private enterprise should take part in government decisions. No sooner does someone leave the ranks of that same enterprise to give the Canadian people, the affairs of state, the benefit of his experience in a certain field, people like the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River rise and with innuendos and insinuations try to prove that there is something wrong somewhere. But he never lays a charge. He only gives innuendos and, frankly speaking, I do not think this is on a level with the kind of parliamentary debates we should hear in the House of Commons.
It has been said that the role of the opposition was to give the kind of show we had before us today. Madam Speaker, I always thought the role of the opposition was to make loyal opposition. In fact, the title of the opposition is "loyal opposition". I always thought it meant intellectually loyal. I was very disappointed about that throughout the day.
Is it really responsible, Madam Speaker, to hold up anonymous affidavits? Is it really responsible to say that there is no difference between allegations, to use the word of the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) when he said this afternoon: True or not?
After all, the Canadian Parliament has become a place where the vilest rumours can be spread and thrown at the people's face without the least evidence. Hon. members opposite have reached the point where they talk about prima facie allegations. I would advise them all to return to their law textbooks or their books on the constitution and political science, and brush up their knowledge. There is no such thing as prima facie allegations but only prima facie evidence. Allegations as such are groundless!
By the way, they are the same members who, on many occasions, have accused reporters of the press gallery of reporting false information at times. I believe they could say in turn: "Have a good look at the members throwing allegations across the House and claiming that those unsubstantiated allegations amount to evidence or point to wrongdoing.
In his brief remarks, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) particularly disagreed with his colleague who put the motion when he said that public confidence in the government was decreasing. He should ask himself what is his own party's responsibility for this situation, because day after day, the only thing opposition parties can do is to criticize thoroughly the government's position without
9310

November 20, 1975
Confidence in Government
making the least positive suggestion or proposing any alternative. No wonder the public finds that opposition parties do not have much to offer and indeed they do not offer much.
Then, the hon. member for Joliette commented that the RCMP had searched Senator Giguere's offices and home. I think it is difficult to claim that government agencies do not do anything. On the contrary, those situations they hold against us are all to the government's credit and show quite clearly that there is no one in Canada who is not equal before the law, that nobody is above it. We had other examples in recent years, namely the action brought against CMHC officers. So, there was never any attempt to try and hyde anything. When there was some evidence that criminal offences had been committed, the government took its responsibilities. There is proof of that once again in the Hamilton case, the Air Canada and Mirabel cases that the RCMP are now investigating.
The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) suggested this afternoon that all those allegations, all those things were embarrassing for the government. I think this is not so. It is not embarrassing for the government to discover that a Crown official or agent might have committed at a certain time a criminal offence. If such was the case, if the evidence-and I stress evidence, not allegations out of nowhere-was brought before the government, on each occasion the government took its responsibilities, brought the persons involved before the courts which then acted according to the provisions of the Criminal Code.
In spite of what the hon. member for Yukon might have said or thought, nobody questioned the right of the hon. member for Central Nova to raise those matters in this House.
But we should really ask ourselves, Madam Speaker, if it was the best thing to do. The RCMP declared they had started their investigation nine months ago already. Nine months ago, Madam Speaker, and the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) has just made public accusations.
Sensationalism is very tempting. The RCMP commissioner regretted that the member did not proceed otherwise and, besides, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) did say this afternoon that in 1963 he had lodged a complaint and put his documents in the hands of law officers of the Crown.
To be efficient an inquiry must often be carried on without the knowledge of the suspected parties. The fleeting publicity made around a good part of this case may have given headlines to the hon. member but then it may also have made it easy to get rid of files and evidence that might have helped throw some light on those matters.
Finally, instead of seeking sensationalism by revealing every day some more information an approach which can only be profitable to the member who wants to make the headlines, to the accused or to the person suspected of some illegal action, Madam Speaker, I think that every member should rather give the information to whom it may concern, as suggested by the Minister of Justice, to the officers of the RCMP so that an official inquiry be carried on.

In fact, all the evidence presented to the government has been referred to the RCMP so they can accomplish the work with the great expertise recognized most of the time by hon. members opposite when they are not indulging in childish political partisanship.
The hon. member for Central Nova also mentioned things that I consider not too serious, things which did not relate to this debate at all. He started mentioning the PTV, passenger transport vehicles in use at Mirabel Airport. He found with a certain smile great relief in the fact that a certain PTV malfunctioned on the opening day of the airport.
Madam Speaker, he even went to the point of criticizing the operators of those PTV's. Those operators come from my area, they are the guys from home, the guys who were hired by Manpower Centres in three constituencies of the Mirabel and Greater Montreal areas. Those guys met every standard required by the Department of Transport, attended the necessary courses to perform their task, and they are now being childishly accused of not being able to perform their work.
I think it is somewhat disgusting to stress the kind of minor incident which was reported by the hon. member for Central Nova. Besides, he talked about Mirabel before and I guess it will not be the last time he will do so. For instance, he said, as the Minister of Transport stressed today, that some difficulty was experienced with respect to runways, and actually the Minister of Transport thoroughly disproved his statement.
That again is another example of a groundless representation, after what the Minister of Transport mentioned to the House this afternoon. But he is not afraid of those unfounded representations to the House. Not in the least.
I might also stress to him the fact that the development and design of Mirabel are the results, Madam Speaker, of the work of thousands of Quebec people and Canadians who are to us, in my area, a striking example of the genius of our province, and we will not have this kind of slander, this kind of libel which he thinks he is entitled to whether true or not, as he said when he mentioned examples this afternoon.
I shall tell him that the House of Commons is not the place for gossip, rumors, libel through anonymous affidavits. Opposition members dare cry out "shame". In my opinion, when a member rises and holds up to the House of Commons, to the members of this House, anonymous affidavits to tarnish the reputations of some people, I think this cry of "shame" does in fact fit opposition members much better.
Madam Speaker, if the hon. member, instead of wishing to enhance his reputation with gossips and rumours, brought forward some evidence of bad conduct, I would be the first one to support and back him up, because I really believe in an honest and just public administration in this country. That is just what we have and unless the hon. member has specific evidence to give us, I think he should wait until he is in position to do do.
Madam Speaker, some members opposite while they like to criticize government members prove by their protests, as soon as we pay them back in their own coin, that it is unacceptable, that in a certain way, members sitting on
November 20, 1975

this side of the House must bear their criticisms whether they are justified or not. Well, I tell them from this side of the House that each time they want to launch attacks as stupid and ridiculous as the debate this afternoon, we will pay them back in their own coin, argument for argument but not like the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), insult for insult, because we on this side of the House do not believe in the kind of language used by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain during this debate, a language which is not to the credit of members opposite. Further, I know very well that a number of them would not support the kind of remarks that were made, the language used this evening by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain.
As far as the hon. member opposite is concerned, I shall wait, I will come to him latter on. I will discuss one by one the attitudes of members opposite, if they will wait. I now come to the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker). In a style exclusive to him, because nobody on this side would imitate it, he said the current situation is horrible, that we have reached the point where the RCMP are making raids in the offices and homes of parliamentarians. And in the same breath the hon. member goes on to say the government is "stonewalling" opposition charges. There is a clear contradiction there. Such inconsistent logic is hidden behind the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton's customary eloquence. And not fearing anything, he said in conclusion it is important an investigation be made on the matter, implicating no investigation is being made. If the RCMP raided a parliamentarian's office, if they are making raids here and there, how is it possible to suggest the government is doing nothing to clear these charges? I believe the hon. member is neither inconsistent or hard of hearing. He concluded in a certain manner, and I might paraphrase him in his own mother tongue: "If there is nothing to hide, open-up".
Finally, what a novel principle! Let us push aside serious investigations, let us open the door now to large public inquests. Let us open the door to insinuations. Let us open the door to innuendoes, charges they themselves called "prima facie allegations". But where then, may I ask, are our most basic principles?
The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) said that procedures before "law offices of the Crown", before officials of the Department of Justice, may lead to abuse. I presume the idea was that maybe the Minister of Justice or the Solicitor General, after investigation by the RCMP, would shelve the latter's report. Frankly, I wonder how far the hon. member has gone, if he believes that kind of thing would be done on this side. The hon. member said this happened before, and in the context of his own indication, since the matter has been made public, he demonstrates such a situation is now impossible. In order that such a thing be true, three things would be required. First, that the Minister of Justice put the lid on the file. Second, that the Solicitor General put the lid on the file. Third, that the RCMP commissioner put the lid on the file.
And finally, the hon. member said that it is precisely what happened. After all, if that had happened, I suppose the file would have been buried, which it has not been.
