subtopic: TRANSPORT-FREIGHT RATES-DISPARITY BETWEEN RATE ON FRESH FRUIT FROM OKANAGAN TO EASTERN CANADA AND RATE FROM STATE OF WASHINGTON
TRANSPORT-FREIGHT RATES-DISPARITY BETWEEN RATE ON FRESH FRUIT FROM OKANAGAN TO EASTERN CANADA AND RATE FROM STATE OF WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the question which I am debating tonight should concern both the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). Because of the disparity between the cost of transportation for fruit, mainly apples, from Washington state to eastern Canada, and Okanagan or Canadian apples to eastern Canada, it probably concerns the Minister of Transport more. However, this sort of problem should concern the Government of Canada as a whole.
The disparity is 43 cents a bushel box in favour of the United States apple growers, This will amount to $318,000 on the almost 890 cars of apples that have to be shipped into eastern Canada if the Okanagan Valley is to sell its large crop that was produced this year.
This is one cent per pound to the apple producer. It may not sound like much, but it is a tremendous amount to the apple producer of the Okanagan Valley, certainly when one realizes that he has to absorb it all. If he is to convince the five remaining apple buyers in eastern Canada to buy his product, he must be competitive especially as to price. With the buying power in so few hands, there is just no question of loyalty to Canadian producers anymore.
The Canadian apple producer must ship to eastern Canada on a delivered basis in order to meet this unfair competitive advantage. It means he must absorb the freight difference. It has to come directly out of his pocket. No one else in the total scheme of things suffers, and it is doubtful if the house wife will get her apples for a cent a pound less.
No wonder the apple producer becomes very upset. Talk about tariffs! Talk about free-trade in Canada! This one operation alone, given the high cost of transportation when

the Canadian railways arbitrarily decide to charge what the traffic will bear, gives our competitors in the United States an advantage that far outweighs any tariff protection we may have ever had. And when I say this, this does not just apply to apples alone in Canada. It also applies to the many other products being manufactured in Canada, especially by the small struggling manufacturer desperately trying to build his business, to keep up and to compete.
A good example of this is the manufacture of parta-board in Grand Forks, British Columbia. This company is struggling to maintain its market in eastern Canada against the freight rate advantage enjoyed by the competition from the United States. There are undoubtedly hundreds of manufacturers in the same position in Canada, whether it be in western Canada or eastern Canada.
Going back to apples, it is no wonder that the balance of trade in apples, Canada versus the United States, has so dramatically changed over the past four years. Four years ago when I left the industry as an official, we were shipping one million boxes of apples to the United States, and the United States was shipping almost one million boxes into Canada a very good balance and one with which we were not too unhappy. However, when one takes a look at the record today, just a short time later, it is astounding to see that the number of boxes of apples coming into Canada is almost three million, or three times what it was four years ago, and the amount of apples shipped from Canada to the United States is going down under the million mark.
I say to the minister, take a look at these records, because there is no doubt that the Canadian railways have to take some of the responsibility for what has happened in this balance of trade. Over the last few years we have been very short of cars to ship to eastern Canada and for export. This could well happen again this year, which would be very disastrous on top of the disparity in freight rates.
I say to the Minister of Transport that when he replies, almost in a sad dejected way, to my question by saying that he has no power over the railways, he had better make strong representation to them to the effect that it is when these companies, or monopolies if you will, fail to perform their functions properly in the best interest of the Canadian people that we must have more government interference.
I do not like to see more government interference or government power applied, but I recognize that it must happen when the Canadian railways are failing the people. When freight rates in Canada become a bigger barrier to Canadian manufacturers than tariffs, the minister must do some in depth soul-searching on this subject. Do not tell us you have no power. The Canadian government is all powerful. Let's not have the feeling that the railways run Canada. Either they do their job properly, or you must get the power so that you can be sure that they do it properly.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-FREIGHT RATES-DISPARITY BETWEEN RATE ON FRESH FRUIT FROM OKANAGAN TO EASTERN CANADA AND RATE FROM STATE OF WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the hon. member no doubt knows, he raises an issue tonight which touches close to my heart as a westerner, and about which pretty well everyone from my part of Canada holds strong views. This evening, as we discuss this subject for which I have a great deal of sympathy, most members in the Cham-
November 20, 1975

ber are either westerners or maritimers. That shows how widespread is the concern on this subject.
Perhaps I can begin to assist my hon friend tonight by relating some background on this most contentious subject of freight rates which is of great interest to Canadians and, certainly, to the government.
For a number of years, as he indicated, the rates on fruit coming out of both the Okanagan Valley and Washington State were at pretty well the same level. Fairly recently, Canadian railways began to increase their rates to a significant extent. As justification, the railways cite increases in costs which have gone up tremendously. They argue that previous rates, even existing rates, do not seem to provide a sufficient return on investment.
To explain the differential between Canada and the United States, the railways point to such cost differences as the spread between the price of a refrigeration car in Canada and the price of the same unit for moving fresh fruit in the United States. Canadian purchases of such equipment cost something in the order of $20,000 more than they do on the American side. In addition, locomotives cost more in Canada. As a result of these factors, and perhaps others, relevant Canadian and U.S. freight rates for fruit coming from the west have started to part in favour of the American grower.
There have been extensive discussions, and probably more will follow-I hope they will-between officials of the Ministry of Transport and of the railways on this topic and, of course, on other freight rate issues.
As the hon. member knows, and as he has stated this evening, under present legislative arrangements the railways have the legal authority to establish rates within certain rules. The railways are, of course, subject to the current economic restraint program and must comply with the guidelines. In particular, I would refer here to the 95 per cent of margin rule. Further restrictions upon specific freight rates such as the hon. member has in mind, or in connection with freight rates generally, would require changes in legislation.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ST. PIERRE-MIQUELON-DISCUSSIONS WITH FRANCE ON DETERMINATION OF OFFSHORE RESOURCE RIGHTS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ST. PIERRE-MIQUELON-DISCUSSIONS WITH FRANCE ON DETERMINATION OF OFFSHORE RESOURCE RIGHTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was hoping the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Baker) would be replying to my question tonight since he comes from my own province which is so lovely. In any case, I hope to get some more response with regard to a question I directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) on November 12, having to do with bilateral discussions between Canada and certain other nations on fisheries matters following the multi-national negotiations which have taken place at various conferences on the Law of the Sea.
It is obvious that bilateral negotiations are going on between Canada and other nations such as Norway, Mexico, the United States, and now these discussions are being extended to include other nations such as Poland, Spain, and Portugal. But what bothers me is the fact that no mention is ever made of any discussions that are taking
Adjournment Debate
place between Canada and France. It is a wonder, because Canada is in the position where even if she wanted to extend unilaterally a 200 mile limit, the French nation has a trump card in that it possesses, sovereignty over St. Pierre-Miquelon, which juts out right in front of Newfoundland. It is not only in that strategic position but more definitely in front of Canada and the North American continent.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs can tell me as often as he wants that he will take my questions as notice because he doesn't have the answers at his fingertips, but he is as well aware as I was when extracting the answers from his department that there are on-going negotiations between his department and the French authorities on the establishment of equidistant boundaries between the Burin peninsula in Newfoundland and the land mass of St. Pierre-Miquelon.
The minister knows as well as I do what is going on, and it smacks of a jellyfish attitude that Canada will not exert her right to demand that a nation with the land mass of Canada should not have to resort to accepting equidistant boundaries with a land mass of such minuscule proportions, and accept the assertion of France which continues to treat Canadians as country cousins.
The islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon lie, at their closest point, 14 nautical miles south of Newfoundland, but the Canadian island known as Little Green Island lies only three miles from the French coastline. Canada's view is that a median line should be drawn between Little Green and St. Pierre, which would put the boundary one and a half miles from the French coast. The French have argued that the boundary should be mid-channel between their islands and the Burin peninsula, which would give no territorial sea at all to Green Island, which is part of Canada.
I could go on and deal with the facts I have extracted from research that I have done, but it is becoming more obvious every day that Canada with its great land mass does not have the guts to say to the French nation, which is treating us like country cousins, that it has a little blob of land close to Canada which is denying Canada's right to extend its limit to 200 miles. Indeed the French are saying that they can extend their limits as of their own right.
One of the things I have not mentioned is Canada's position as it concerns France, which should be of more importance than geography. France did not invite Canada to the economic conference of six nations, and France still owes us a bill of $11 million when they kicked us out of their NATO bases. It is now 1975 and we do not have the guts to demand payment of the bill. The only excuse the government gives is that it is waiting to see what the United States is going to do about its $100 million bill and the bill of the United Nations amounting to $380 million.
I can only deplore the position Canada is taking in allowing this little blob of land, ten miles by ten, to deny our rights to protect the mineral resources of this country, a matter so important to the province of Newfoundland and to the oil resources off the shores of Newfoundland. We are allowing this nation to hold this over our heads and demand what they can of the North American continent.

November 20, 1975
Adjournment Debate
To me the whole situation smacks of stupidity. It is ridiculous, and makes Canada look like an embarrassed little dot in the eyes of the world.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ST. PIERRE-MIQUELON-DISCUSSIONS WITH FRANCE ON DETERMINATION OF OFFSHORE RESOURCE RIGHTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to reply to the hon. member. I do so, of course, on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) and his parliamentary secretary. May I begin by extending to the hon. member the regret of the minister and his parliamentary secretary at being unable to be present this evening to respond directly to the hon. member's concerns.
I should like to advise the House on the status of our negotiations with France concerning the delimitation of the continental shelf in the area off the islands of St. Pierre et Miquelon. With respect to the narrow waters lying directly between the north and eastern coasts of the St. Pierre and Miquelon islands and the Newfoundland mainland, the agreement between Canada and France on their mutual fishing relations which came into force in March, 1972, provides for a delimitation line between the territorial waters of Canada and the zones submitted to the fishery jurisdiction of France. Negotiations between Canada and France were held in 1972 with respect to the delimitation of the continental shelf in the area to the south of the French islands, but these negotiations have proven inconclusive for the time being.
Following the conclusion of the Law of the Sea Conference, both sides will have more time to pursue further negotiations and hopefully arrive at a satisfactory resolution of this question.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS WITH REGARD TO USE OF CANADIAN SHIPS TO MOVE OIL FROM ARCTIC
TRANSPORT-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS WITH REGARD TO USE OF CANADIAN SHIPS TO MOVE OIL FROM ARCTIC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, concern over the presence in Canada of Arctic vessels other than those of Canadian ownership carrying Canadian crews prompted me the other day, as it has other hon. members of the House, to question the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) with respect to assurances that the government was giving consideration to introducing legislation that would have the effect of requiring removal of natural resources from the Canadian Arctic by Canadian ships of Canadian registry.
For ten years that I can remember in this House such an undertaking has been the expressed concern of myself and, as I mentioned, of many others. In recent years we have had the assurance of ministers such as the immediate past occupant of that portfolio that such, indeed, was the desired objective. Indeed tomorrow, if all goes well, we should have before the House for second reading the new, and I suggest most welcome, maritime code legislation.
What gives rise to apprehension is the absence of any direction in this new bill dealing with the question of closing the area north of 60 degrees by way of legislative action.
The question was prompted by the efforts, for example, of Panarctic to secure from outside Canada the type of ship which would be capable of transporting liquid natural gas from the Arctic to the eastern seaboard. That is not to

mention plans that are currently on-going in the United States for the transportation of oil and other resources out of the Arctic, that portion that lies contiguous to U.S. soil, eastward through the northwest passage and then down the eastern seaboard to U.S. refineries.
Having regard to the intention in respect of the north, I could go through a long series of correspondence. As recently as the end of July the former minister of transport, after a long explanation as to why we had not done anything particular at this point in time, went on to say in a letter signed by him:
-it would be less than realistic for me to suggest that we could, at the present time, envisage a policy which banned under any circumstances, any importation whatsoever of any vessel-or technology for any vessel-destined for use in the Canadian Arctic.
That is going a little bit far and I do not think anybody would really suggest that. What we are really going after is what was suggested by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) on October 25, as reported in the Calgary Albertan. The minister was speaking to some 300 businessmen at a conference on the north. He said the following, and I will quote only the pertinent parts. He said government policy was intended to:
"-achieve more substantial" results in the effort to keep the benefit of northern development in Canada.
In particular he said he would:
Increase the purchase of equipment and services for development from Canadian firms;
Increase the "participation of firms beneficially owned and controlled" by Canadians;
Encourage resource companies "to rationalize their sourcing purchasing in Canada for their world operations."
It is more along these lines that those in the House who have some concern for development in the north rise to seek assurances and commitments from the government that it indeed will go in this direction.
No one expects Canada to be able to supply our shipping needs over night. There are interim periods of adjustment which have to be made. The provisions for the orderly issuance of permits for the orderly development of an operational capability have to be taken into consideration. We are aware of the need for co-operation, and we are aware of the need to look elsewhere from time to time for certain types of expertise. However, we appear not only to ourselves here in this Chamber, but to those throughout the world, to be ignoring the potential of the Arctic. One of our first steps must surely be to require that after a certain date, probably 1985, no resources should be removed by water from Canada's northern waters other than in Canadian-built, beneficially Canadian-owned and Canadian crewed ships. This is the least that is acceptable to Canadians.
To fail in this will be to abandon to foreign cartels the benefits of "first in" in respect of extractive industry in the north. Surely the government recognizes the position of the shipping community in this regard. Give the Canadian shipping community a reason to start planning and it will act. Here in Canada we have the technology and the expertise; we have the capacity to raise the fundings, the capacity to expand our shipyards to accommodate the required building program, and we have the capacity to produce the trained crews. In spite of what some may
November 20, 1975

think, we have a highly stable seafaring labour pool. I say "stable" in the sense that no strikes have occurred, for example, in the SIU since the departure from our shores of Hal Banks.
I will simply call upon the parliamentary secretary and the government to serve notice that it is in fact our intention to move in this direction, that it is our intention to bar foreign shipping from these northern waters. I call upon the government to prepare legislation for submission to parliament during this session, and not waste four or five more years while we lose the opportunity. I say that where we need foreign expertise and help let us get it, and where we need co-operation let us have co-operation, but whatever we do let us give notice to the world that it is our intention to protect the extractive industry for ourselves.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS WITH REGARD TO USE OF CANADIAN SHIPS TO MOVE OIL FROM ARCTIC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, recently there has been discussion in the House concerning the use of Canadian ships in the Arctic, at which time the minister replied to certain queries posed by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall). In view of the interest which has been expressed, it is apparent that a somewhat more detailed response might be of value to the House.
The matter of Arctic shipping is an important area, and new policies to assist Canadian shipping were announced in the Speech from the Throne and in the statement of new transportation policies for frontier areas of Canada. The general theme has been one of the need to encourage Canadian ship operators, builders, and designers to take initiatives and develop the new technology and operating skills for future large scale developments. The most direct and meaningful development is that of the Arctic "Class 2" icebreaking cargo vessel, to be built and operated by the Canadian shipping industry with government participation and financial support.
I am pleased to be able to report that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) made an announcement on this very project just this afternoon. This particular vessel, which
Adjournment Debate
will be called the MV Arctic, a famous name in the annals of exploration of the Canadian Arctic, is a bulk carrier designed to operate in the high Arctic where two lead zinc mines are now in different stages of development. The Strathcona Mine on Strathcona Sound is due to come on stream in 1978-79. The Canadian government has an 18 per cent share in this mine. The second mine, at Little Cornwallis, so called the Polaris Project by Cominco, is presently seeking an export permit and is due to begin export in 1978-79 also.
There is no explicit policy which requires the use of Canadian vessels for movement of goods or minerals out of Canada, as there is for the coasting trade. However, in the granting of export permits both the mineral mines mentioned will be required to offer, if available, a proportion of their production to Canadian ships. It should also be noted that Bill C-61, the Maritime Code Act, which is now before the House, contains additional provisions to reserve the coasting trade for Canadian shipping.
Officials of the Ministry of Transport, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and INA are presently working on the matter of transportation and related industrial benefits associated with this element of resource development. The MV Arctic was conceived and supported by private industry, Federal Commerce and Navigation, with the co-operation of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Ministry of Transport. This support was based on the need to encourage the construction of Arctic ships which are more expensive than normal vessels, for early mineral developments, and to use this ship as a model or prototype of larger vessels for movement of oil and gas out of the Arctic to southern Canada to meet future energy requirements.
Such requirements are becoming more urgent and the consensus is that only ships can be used, at least initially, to move the oil to market. The transportation of oil from the Arctic Islands, or an offshore island in the Arctic, to the Canadian mainland is subject to the new coasting trade laws and as such the cargo will be reserved to Canadian-flag vessels.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.26 p.m.

Friday, November 21, 1975
